title: Pelvic HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin: a case report
abstract: Background Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a rare subtype of malignant tumor. When it presents as pelvic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the difficulty of clinical diagnosis and treatment increases significantly. Notably, some such pelvic SCC cases are confirmed to be associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, yet the primary tumor remains unidentified despite systematic imaging evaluation, endoscopy, and pathological biopsy. Currently, there is no unified consensus on the diagnostic criteria, therapeutic strategies, and prognostic assessment of this specific clinical entity, which has become one of the urgent problems to be solved in oncology. Case presentation A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman was admitted with urinary discomfort and lower abdominal distension for 15 days. Physical examination revealed a fixed, non-tender solid pelvic mass in the left lower abdomen. Laboratory testing showed an elevated serum squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC-Ag) level of 9.11 ng/mL, while other tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 125, were within normal ranges. Transvaginal ultrasonography and 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass in the left pelvis. To investigate the primary site, comprehensive evaluation including cervical HPV testing and cytology, colonoscopy, and cystoscopy was performed, but no definite primary malignant lesion was identified. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the pelvic mass showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Exploratory laparotomy was subsequently performed, and postoperative histopathological examination confirmed moderately to well-differentiated invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Diffuse strong p16 expression together with positive tumor HPV E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supported an HPV-associated tumor phenotype. Although lymph node metastasis was suspected intraoperatively, no definite lymph node metastasis was confirmed by pathological examination. Conclusion This case describes a rare HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin in which no definite primary malignancy was identified in the cervix, other lower genital tract sites, gastrointestinal tract, or urinary tract after comprehensive evaluation. The case highlights the diagnostic value of integrating imaging, endoscopic assessment, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and tumor-based HPV testing in patients with pelvic SCC of uncertain origin. Importantly, the absence of a detectable mucosal primary site should not be interpreted as evidence of a primary pelvic origin. Instead, occult mucosal disease and other potential primary sites should remain diagnostic considerations. Further accumulation of similar cases and longer follow-up are needed to clarify the biological origin and optimal management of this rare clinical presentation.

source_records.title: Pelvic HPV-associated squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin: a case report
source_records.abstract: Background Cancer of unknown primary (CUP) is a rare subtype of malignant tumor. When it presents as pelvic squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the difficulty of clinical diagnosis and treatment increases significantly. Notably, some such pelvic SCC cases are confirmed to be associated with human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, yet the primary tumor remains unidentified despite systematic imaging evaluation, endoscopy, and pathological biopsy. Currently, there is no unified consensus on the diagnostic criteria, therapeutic strategies, and prognostic assessment of this specific clinical entity, which has become one of the urgent problems to be solved in oncology. Case presentation A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman was admitted with urinary discomfort and lower abdominal distension for 15 days. Physical examination revealed a fixed, non-tender solid pelvic mass in the left lower abdomen. Laboratory testing showed an elevated serum squamous cell carcinoma antigen (SCC-Ag) level of 9.11 ng/mL, while other tumor markers, including carcinoembryonic antigen and carbohydrate antigen 125, were within normal ranges. Transvaginal ultrasonography and 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography ( 18 F-FDG-PET/CT) demonstrated a hypermetabolic mass in the left pelvis. To investigate the primary site, comprehensive evaluation including cervical HPV testing and cytology, colonoscopy, and cystoscopy was performed, but no definite primary malignant lesion was identified. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous biopsy of the pelvic mass showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Exploratory laparotomy was subsequently performed, and postoperative histopathological examination confirmed moderately to well-differentiated invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Diffuse strong p16 expression together with positive tumor HPV E6/E7 mRNA in situ hybridization supported an HPV-associated tumor phenotype. Although lymph node metastasis was suspected intraoperatively, no definite lymph node metastasis was confirmed by pathological examination. Conclusion This case describes a rare HPV-associated pelvic squamous cell carcinoma of unknown primary origin in which no definite primary malignancy was identified in the cervix, other lower genital tract sites, gastrointestinal tract, or urinary tract after comprehensive evaluation. The case highlights the diagnostic value of integrating imaging, endoscopic assessment, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and tumor-based HPV testing in patients with pelvic SCC of uncertain origin. Importantly, the absence of a detectable mucosal primary site should not be interpreted as evidence of a primary pelvic origin. Instead, occult mucosal disease and other potential primary sites should remain diagnostic considerations. Further accumulation of similar cases and longer follow-up are needed to clarify the biological origin and optimal management of this rare clinical presentation.

title: HPV-associated extracellular vesicles and the tumor microenvironment: mechanisms of immune modulation and translational implications
abstract: Human papillomavirus infections are a major cause of cervical cancer and are also associated with several anogenital and oropharyngeal malignancies. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types and sustained expression of viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 contribute to malignant transformation. Extracellular vesicles are increasingly recognized as important mediators of intercellular communication and can transfer proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and other regulatory molecules between cells. HPV-associated changes in EV cargo, such as viral transcripts, may influence immune and stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment. Experimental studies have implicated HPV-associated EVs in the regulation of dendritic cell function, macrophage polarization, T-cell responses, immune checkpoint signaling, chronic inflammation, and mechanisms related to viral persistence and immune evasion. Cell-based and preclinical studies also suggest that EVs released by HPV-positive tumor cells may contribute to related disorders including angiogenesis and metastatic progression. On the other hand, human studies have primarily provided observational evidence linking EV-associated molecular profiles with HPV status or disease characteristics. Beyond these mechanistic insights, a growing body of work explores the translational potential of EVs, including their use as liquid-biopsy biomarkers and as engineered delivery platforms such as Nefmut-based vesicles carrying HPV16 E7 that elicit protective CD8 + T-cell responses in preclinical models. This narrative review, with emphasis on tumor-immune interactions, and also discusses emerging diagnostic and therapeutic applications together with the methodological and clinical barriers that must be addressed before EV-based strategies can be translated into routine practice.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on the role of human papillomaviruses (HPV) in the tumor microenvironment, particularly their association with cervical cancer and other malignancies. It highlights the mechanisms by which HPV-associated extracellular vesicles (EVs) modulate immune responses, including effects on dendritic cells, macrophages, and T-cell activity. The review also discusses the potential of EVs as biomarkers and therapeutic tools, such as engineered Nefmut-based vesicles carrying HPV16 E7. However, it notes that human studies have mainly provided observational evidence, and there are gaps in understanding the full impact of EVs on disease progression and immune evasion. The review emphasizes the need to address methodological and clinical challenges before EV-based strategies can be applied in routine practice.

title: HPV Knowledge, Vaccination Awareness, and the Knowledge–Practice Gap in Cervical Cancer Prevention Among Turkish Women: A Cross-Sectional Study
abstract: Background/Objectives: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and cervical cancer screening are key components of cervical cancer prevention; however, awareness may not translate into preventive practice. This study aimed to assess HPV knowledge, HPV vaccine awareness and uptake, Pap smear testing history, and sociodemographic factors associated with HPV knowledge among women attending a gynecology outpatient clinic in Türkiye. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 403 women aged 18–49 years who attended the Gynecology and Obstetrics Outpatient Clinic of Konya City Hospital between July and October 2025. Following a brief explanation of the study, participants independently completed self-administered questionnaires, including a demographic questionnaire and the validated Turkish HPV Knowledge Scale (HPV-KS). Group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests, with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons where appropriate. An exploratory multivariable binary logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with having any HPV knowledge (HPV-KS > 0). Results: The median total HPV-KS score was 8 (Q1–Q3: 0–15). Overall, 52.6% of participants had heard of HPV and 44.2% had heard of the HPV vaccine, whereas 18.9% reported previous Pap smear testing and only 3.2% reported HPV vaccination. Knowledge of HPV vaccine availability/use was particularly limited, with a median score of 0 (Q1–Q3: 0–1). Total HPV-KS scores were significantly higher among women with university education, employment, urban residence, contraceptive use, previous Pap smear testing, and prior awareness of HPV or the HPV vaccine (p < 0.05). In the multivariable analysis, compared with university graduates, participants with primary-level education (aOR = 0.26, 95% CI: 0.14–0.49) and high-school education (aOR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.25–0.70) had lower odds of having any HPV knowledge, whereas employment (aOR = 2.45, 95% CI: 1.41–4.23) and previous Pap smear testing (aOR = 4.38, 95% CI: 2.05–9.36) were associated with higher odds. Conclusions: HPV and vaccine awareness exceeded reported vaccination and Pap smear testing uptake, although awareness itself remained limited. Particularly low knowledge of HPV vaccine availability/use highlights an actionable knowledge gap. Educational and healthcare-contact factors were associated with HPV knowledge, supporting accessible counseling that provides practical information on vaccine eligibility, schedules, access, and cervical cancer prevention.

title: High Second-Year Immunisation Coverage Alongside Persistent Newer Vaccine Hesitancy: A Mixed-Methods Study in Three Districts of Malawi
abstract: Background/Objectives: Vaccines delivered after infancy remain vulnerable to missed uptake. Less is known about the determinants of second-year-of-life vaccine uptake in Malawi. This study assessed the completion of vaccines due after 12 months of age, caregiver confidence in newer vaccines, and associated factors in three districts of Malawi. Methods: A mixed-methods cross-sectional study surveyed 1177 caregivers. Logistic regression examined factors associated with caregiver-reported completion of vaccines due after 12 months among age-eligible children. Focus group discussions with caregivers and key-informant interviews with community volunteers and leaders were then analysed thematically to explain the survey findings. Results: Among 1287 age-eligible children, 94.2% completed second-year vaccines, although coverage of the Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine was lower. Distance over 5 kilometres from a facility was associated with lower odds of completion, while health worker reminders were associated with higher odds of vaccine completion (adjusted odds ratio 3.03, 95% confidence interval 1.61 to 5.88). Qualitative accounts highlighted defaulter tracing and infertility concerns about HPV (22.2%). Conclusions: Second-year coverage was high among caregivers reached by immunisation services, but distance and lower uptake of newer vaccines remained important gaps. Strengthening geographical access, communication about newer vaccines, and adequately resourced health-worker follow-up may improve completion.

title: Clinical and sonographic characteristics of gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma: a descriptive case series of 13 patients
abstract: Objective Gastric-type endocervical adenocarcinoma (G-EAC) is a distinct human papillomavirus (HPV)-independent subtype of cervical adenocarcinoma for which early diagnosis continues to pose a clinical challenge. We set out to characterize the clinical and sonographic features of G-EAC and to provide hypothesis-generating observations to guide future research. Methods This retrospective analysis comprised 13 patients with histopathologically confirmed G-EAC who underwent surgery at our center between August 2017 and September 2024. We reviewed and descriptively summarized the clinical presentation, HPV and cytology results, cervical biopsy findings, tumor markers, and ultrasonographic and cross-sectional imaging findings, together with all available pathological and surgical records. Results The patients were aged 39–76 years (mean, 53.4 years), and all were parous. Vaginal discharge was the most common presenting symptom (8/13, 61.5%), followed by irregular vaginal bleeding (4/13, 30.8%) and postcoital bleeding (1/13, 7.7%). HPV testing was negative in 11/13 patients (84.6%); 1/13 (7.7%) tested positive for HPV 58, and another 1/13 (7.7%) carried a different high-risk HPV type. ThinPrep cytologic testing (TCT) was negative in 12/13 patients (92.3%), whereas atypical squamous cells were detected in 1/13 (7.7%). Among the 11 patients who underwent colposcopy with cervical biopsy, histopathological findings were negative in 8/11 (72.7%), mild glandular atypia was identified in 2/11 (18.2%), and rare adenocarcinoma cells were identified in 1/11 (9.1%). All 13 patients underwent preoperative ultrasound. Ultrasound findings raised suspicion of cervical malignancy in 9/13 patients (69.2%), were suggestive of benign cervical cystic lesions in 2/13 (15.4%), and were unremarkable in the remaining 2/13 (15.4%). A honeycomb sonographic pattern was present in 7/13 patients (53.8%), and abundant intralesional vascularity (Adler grade III) was present in 9/13 patients (69.2%). Preoperative MRI was performed in 10/13 patients (76.9%), 1 of whom also underwent CT, whereas the remaining 3/13 patients (23.1%) underwent neither MRI nor CT. A barrel-shaped cervix was documented in the pathological or surgical records of 4/13 patients (30.8%). Conclusion G-EAC may come to attention through a combination of clinical and imaging findings that together raise diagnostic suspicion. In this series, HPV negativity was common, and vaginal discharge was the most frequent presenting complaint. A honeycomb sonographic pattern and abundant intralesional vascularity may raise suspicion of G-EAC, although these findings remain descriptive and require validation in larger, adequately controlled studies.

title: Cervical cancer: A cross-sectional study of knowledge, attitudes, perceptions, and barriers to screening and prevention among female university students
abstract: A total of 277 female students from 11 specialties participated in an online cross-sectional survey at the Medical University of Sofia. Differences between specialties were observed in knowledge of human papillomavirus transmission, understanding of Pap smear results, testing practices, and vaccination. Despite generally satisfactory awareness, gaps in preventive knowledge and practices remained among some student groups. Lack of time, insufficient information, fear, and embarrassment were identified as the main barriers to screening. Regression analysis identified specialty, age, year of study, parental education, place of residence, and understanding of Pap smear results as factors associated with variations in knowledge and preventive practices. The findings indicate that health-related education alone does not ensure consistent preventive behavior. More targeted and comprehensive educational interventions addressing human papillomavirus, screening, and vaccination may strengthen preventive practices among future healthcare professionals.

title: Synchronous presacral schwannoma and carcinoma cervix: A rare diagnostic and therapeutic dilemma.
abstract: Schwannomas are benign, encapsulated tumors originating from Schwann cells of the peripheral nervous system. Pelvic and presacral schwannomas are rare, often clinically silent, and are frequently diagnosed incidentally or when they attain sufficient size to compress adjacent pelvic structures. Synchronous occurrence of a presacral schwannoma with cervical carcinoma in the same patient is exceptionally rare and poses significant diagnostic and management challenges. We present a 65-year-old postmenopausal woman (P7L7A1) who presented with per vaginal bleeding and was subsequently diagnosed with simultaneous FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) Stage IIIB carcinoma cervix and a 5.3 cm presacral pelvic mass. Biopsy of the cervical lesion confirmed squamous cell carcinoma (p16-positive, human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated). Repeat core needle biopsy of the presacral mass, followed by immunohistochemistry demonstrating strong S100 protein and SOX10 positivity, confirmed schwannoma. A multidisciplinary tumor board decided to prioritise treatment of the malignancy. The patient received definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (EBRT 50.4 Gy + concurrent cisplatin) followed by three sessions of high-dose rate intracavitary brachytherapy (7 Gy per fraction). Post-treatment imaging revealed excellent local response at the cervix, whereas the schwannoma demonstrated interval growth to 6.5 × 6.4 cm. Surgical resection of the schwannoma was planned following adequate recovery from radiation sequelae. This case highlights the importance of thorough diagnostic workup for incidentally detected pelvic masses in patients with gynecological malignancies, the value of multidisciplinary team discussion in prioritising competing pathologies, and the need to carefully consider how treatment of one pathology may affect the future management of the other.

title: HPV E6/E7, O-GlcNAcylation and mitochondrial remodeling in cervical cancer: mechanistic links and translational opportunities
abstract: Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection initiates cervical carcinogenesis, while progression and treatment resistance also involve metabolic adaptation. O-GlcNAcylation is a reversible post-translational modification (PTM) controlled by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and O-GlcNAcase (OGA), with UDP-GlcNAc generated by the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway (HBP) serving as the donor substrate. This review evaluates evidence linking HPV E6/E7-associated metabolic demand, HBP flux, O-GlcNAcylation, and mitochondrial function. We distinguish observations made under untreated conditions from acute treatment responses, identify whether validated resistant models were used, and examine HPV genotype as a source of heterogeneity. Cervical cancer studies support links between O-GlcNAcylation and pathways involved in growth and survival, but no mitochondrial O-GlcNAcylation site has been causally validated in HPV-positive cervical cancer. We therefore grade evidence by model, temporal context, and causal depth and place the proposed relationships within a broader PTM network. This synthesis separates findings obtained in cervical cancer from mechanisms inferred from other systems and identifies the main gaps limiting biomarker and therapeutic development.

title: Expression of CDKN2A Gene for Early Detection of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma - An Evaluative Study.
abstract: AIM AND OBJECTIVES: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is difficult to detect at an early stage using routine imaging or biopsy. Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A ( CDKN2A ) is a major tumour-suppressor gene in OSCC, and alterations in its gene expression reflect early molecular changes during carcinogenesis. This study aims to evaluate CDKN2A gene expression in untreated early-stage OSCC patients and assess its potential relevance for early disease detection. METHODOLOGY: Sixty participants (30 early-stage OSCC patients and 30 matched healthy controls) were included. From OSCC patients, ribonucleic acid (RNA) was isolated from matched tumour and adjacent normal mucosal tissues. CDKN2A gene expression levels were quantified using quantitative reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction with normalisation to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH). Human papillomavirus status and clinical features were assessed to interpret biomarker performance. Statistical analysis used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for paired tissue data, with P < 0.05 considered significant. RESULTS: CDKN2A mRNA expression was significantly lower in OSCC tumour tissue than in adjacent normal mucosa in the present cohort (median 0.65 vs 1.15, P < 0.05). The Cancer Genome Atlas head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) data ( n = 520) showed higher CDKN2A transcript levels in tumours compared with normal tissues. However, oral cavity-specific analysis showed no significant difference ( P = 0.693), which was similar to the findings observed in HPV-negative oral tumours in the present study. CONCLUSION: CDKN2A mRNA is significantly downregulated in early-stage HPV-negative OSCC tissue and may serve as a tissue-based molecular marker. Biofluid CDKN2A mRNA shows low sensitivity for non-invasive screening. Larger cohorts and multi-marker panels may improve its diagnostic performance and clinical utility in early detection.

title: Lactobacillus crispatus FY121-Derived Extracellular Vesicles Suppress HPV-Positive Cervical Cancer Cells and Activate RIG-I/MAVS/IRF3 Signaling
abstract: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is the major cause of cervical cancer (CC), and viral oncogenes E6 and E7 contribute to tumor progression by promoting malignant transformation and impairing innate immune responses. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) derived from beneficial bacteria have emerged as potential regulators of host cellular functions. However, their role in HPV-associated cervical cancer remains unclear. In this study, we isolated and characterized extracellular vesicles derived from Lactobacillus crispatus FY121 (LcEVs) and investigated their effects on HPV-positive cervical cancer cell lines. LcEVs were efficiently internalized by HPV16-positive SiHa and HPV18-positive HeLa cells and significantly suppressed cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Furthermore, LcEVs reduced HPV E6 and E7 expression at both the transcriptional and protein levels. Mechanistically, LcEV treatment was associated with increased RIG-I/MAVS/IRF3 signaling and enhanced IFN-β transcription and secretion. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad alterations in immune-related and cellular functional programs following LcEV treatment. In a co-injection xenograft model, LcEVs reduced tumor establishment and early outgrowth of HPV-positive cervical cancer cells and were accompanied by increased RIG-I/MAVS/IRF3 signaling in tumor tissue. Proteomic profiling identified diverse functional proteins within LcEVs, providing potential molecular candidates underlying their biological effects. Together, these results show that LcEVs suppress the malignant phenotypes of HPV-positive cervical cancer cells and are accompanied by activation of nucleic acid sensing and type I interferon signaling in vitro and in vivo. The identity of the active vesicular cargo and its causal contribution to these effects remain to be established, and bacterial EVs are highlighted as candidate immunomodulatory agents for HPV-related malignancies.

Together, these results show that LcEVs suppress the malignant phenotypes of HPV-positive cervical cancer cells and are accompanied by activation of nucleic acid sensing and type I interferon signaling in vitro and in vivo. title: Immediate histopathological outcomes according to Aptima HPV E6/E7 mRNA genotype, age, and menopausal status in women with ASC-H/HSIL cytology
abstract: Objective To examine the associations of Aptima HPV E6/E7 mRNA genotype, age, and menopausal status with immediate histopathological outcomes in women with ASC-H/HSIL cytology. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 330 women aged 20–84 years with ASC-H/HSIL cytology who underwent Aptima HPV testing, colposcopy-guided biopsy, and histopathological examination. Histopathological outcomes were compared according to hrHPV genotype, age, and menopausal status. Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate the associations of hrHPV genotype, age, and menopausal status with CIN2 +. Results Among women with ASC-H/HSIL cytology, 38.2% had cervical precancerous lesions and 24.5% had malignant lesions. HPV16 and the other 11 hrHPV types were associated with a higher prevalence of CIN2/3, while HPV16-positive women had the highest prevalence of SCC. Both AIS cases occurred in the HPV18/45-positive group, although this subgroup was small. CIN2/3 prevalence decreased with age, whereas SCC prevalence increased. In the multivariable analysis, HPV16, HPV18/45, and the other 11 hrHPV types were independently associated with CIN2+, whereas age and menopausal status were not. Conclusions Histopathological outcomes among women with ASC-H/HSIL cytology differed according to hrHPV genotype. HPV16 positivity was strongly associated with cervical precancerous and malignant lesions. Age and menopausal status showed differences in unadjusted analyses but were not independently associated with CIN2 +.

title: Assessing an educational strategy to improve community health provider-led provision of cervical cancer screening services in western Kenya: A secondary analysis of the Elimisha-HPV cluster-randomized controlled trial.
abstract: Cervical cancer disproportionately impacts women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where over 90% of global cervical cancer deaths occur. Lay health workers, such as community health promoters (CHPs), with appropriate training and support, can play a pivotal role in cervical cancer prevention. Our team developed a multi-level intervention, Elimisha-HPV, to support CHP-delivered human papillomavirus (HPV) testing in Kenya. The present analysis evaluates impact of Elimisha-HPV on the following CHP outcomes: i) knowledge of screening delivery and privacy, confidentiality, and professionalism; ii) stigma associated with cervical cancer, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and HPV; and iii) confidence to counsel in screening delivery. We used descriptive statistics and linear mixed effects regression models to evaluate intervention effects (intervention group, n = 64; control group, n = 60). For knowledge and privacy, no statistically significant effects were observed (knowledge: β= -0.08 [95% CI, -0.22 to 0.07]; privacy: β= 0.04 [95% CI, -0.05 to 0.13]). For the confidence to counsel Likert scale-style questions, evaluated using descriptive and regression approaches, proportional increases were observed across both arms, but the main effect was not statistically significant ( β= 0.01 [95% CI, -0.09 to 0.11]). Our findings align with previous work demonstrating that stigma surrounding cervical cancer in LMICs is difficult to effectively influence, and provide a foundation for shaping future stigma-reduction campaigns. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05736588.

title: Non-invasive biomarkers of oral and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: a quantitative synthesis of data on diagnostic and prognostic value
abstract: The high incidence of and mortality from oral and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, together with the limitations of conventional diagnostic and surveillance methods, highlight the need for objective, non-invasive, and accessible biomarkers for early detection and prognostic assessment. To systematically review and quantitatively assess the diagnostic and prognostic value of non-invasive biomarkers for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal cancer, and to evaluate the quality of the available studies. Materials and methods . The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines, published in 2021. PubMed/MEDLINE, eLibrary, CyberLeninka, and Google Scholar were searched for publications dated January 1, 2021, through April 5, 2026, using combinations of Russian and English keywords, including Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). Eligible human studies included patients with histologically confirmed OSCC or HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, patients with precancerous lesions (leukoplakia or erythroplakia), or healthy controls; assessed biomarkers in saliva, oral fluid, plasma, or serum; and reported quantitative measures of diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, or area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) or prognostic performance (hazard ratio [HR], positive predictive value [PPV], or negative predictive value [NPV]). Study quality was assessed using QUADAS-2 and the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Two reviewers independently performed study selection and data extraction. Seven studies of high or moderate quality, with sample sizes ranging from 48 to 1,076 participants, were included. Salivary podoplanin differentiated OSCC from leukoplakia and healthy controls with an AUC of 0.987, a sensitivity of 93.3%, and a specificity of 95%. p16 immunohistochemistry identified transcriptionally active HPV with a sensitivity of 95.9% and a specificity of 90.5%, using HPV messenger RNA as the reference standard. Salivary CD44 and total protein were predictors of recurrence (adjusted HRs of 1.13 and 3.51, respectively). In one study, plasma tumor tissue-modified viral HPV DNA (TTMV-HPV DNA) testing yielded a PPV and NPV of 95% each. In another study, sensitivity was 73%, specificity was 98%, and the HR was 75. Rising anti-E7 antibody titers predicted death or recurrence with a specificity of 100% and a sensitivity of 36%. PCR-based detection of HPV-16 DNA in plasma and saliva yielded a sensitivity of 65%, a specificity of 87%, and an HR of 13.15. The biomarkers assessed, including podoplanin, CD44, TTMV-HPV DNA, anti-E7 antibodies, and p16, have high diagnostic and prognostic value. Particularly promising results were reported for TTMV-HPV DNA testing in recurrence surveillance, with PPV reaching 95% and NPV reaching 97%, and for podoplanin in early diagnosis, with an AUC exceeding 0.97. However, large prospective studies are needed to standardize cutoffs, validate these tests in routine clinical practice, and assess their impact on survival before they can be incorporated into clinical guidelines.

To systematically review and quantitatively assess the diagnostic and prognostic value of non-invasive biomarkers for oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal cancer, and to evaluate the quality of the available studies. Materials and methods . The review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines, published in 2021. PubMed/MEDLINE, eLibrary, CyberLeninka, and Google Scholar were searched for publications dated January 1, 2021, through April 5, 2026, using combinations of Russian and English keywords, including Medical Subject Headings (MeSH). Eligible human studies included patients with histologically confirmed OSCC or HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, patients with precancerous lesions (leukoplakia or erythroplakia), or healthy controls; assessed biomarkers in saliva, oral fluid, plasma, or serum; and reported quantitative measures of diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity, specificity, or area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC]) or prognostic performance (hazard ratio [HR], positive predictive value [PPV], or negative predictive value [NPV]). Study quality was assessed using QUADAS-2 and the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Two reviewers independently performed study selection and data extraction. Seven studies of high or moderate quality, with sample sizes ranging from 48 to 1,076 participants, were included. Salivary podoplanin differentiated OSCC from leukoplakia and healthy controls with an AUC of 0.987, a sensitivity of 93.3%, and a specificity of 95%. p16 immunohistochemistry identified transcriptionally active HPV with a sensitivity of 95.9% and a specificity of 90.5%, using HPV messenger RNA as the reference standard. Salivary CD44 and total protein were predictors of recurrence (adjusted HRs of 1.13 and 3.51, respectively). In one study, plasma tumor tissue-modified viral HPV DNA (TTMV-HPV DNA) testing yielded a PPV and NPV of 95% each. In another study, sensitivity was 73%, specificity was 98%, and the HR was 75. Rising anti-E7 antibody titers predicted death or recurrence with a specificity of 100% and a sensitivity of 36%. PCR-based detection of HPV-16 DNA in plasma and saliva yielded a sensitivity of 65%, a specificity of 87%, and an HR of 13.15. The biomarkers assessed, including podoplanin, CD44, TTMV-HPV DNA, anti-E7 antibodies, and p16, have high diagnostic and prognostic value. Particularly promising results were reported for TTMV-HPV DNA testing in recurrence surveillance, with PPV reaching 95% and NPV reaching 97%, and for podoplanin in early diagnosis, with an AUC exceeding 0.97. However, large prospective studies are needed to standardize cutoffs, validate these tests in routine clinical practice, and assess their impact on survival before they can be incorporated into clinical guidelines.

title: HPV prevalence and genotype distribution in rare cervical adenocarcinoma subtypes: A 10-year retrospective cohort study from Brazil
abstract: Objectives This study aimed primarily to determine human papillomavirus prevalence and genotype distribution in rare cervical adenocarcinoma subtypes. Secondary objectives were to evaluate associations between human papillomavirus status, clinicopathological characteristics, and survival outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort included patients with rare cervical adenocarcinoma subtypes treated at the Brazilian National Cancer Institute between 2011 and 2021. Human papillomavirus deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) detection and genotyping were performed in histopathological samples. Results Among 107 patients, the median age at diagnosis was 44.00 years (interquartile range 37.00, 52.50). Tumor samples from 88 patients were available for human papillomavirus DNA analysis, of which 78 (88.64%) were positive. Genotype 16 (69.23%) was the predominant genotype. Non-mucinous adenocarcinomas were associated with poorer overall survival (HR 4.77; 95% CI 1.78, 12.76), whereas human papillomavirus status was not significantly associated with survival outcomes. Conclusion Human papillomavirus DNA positivity was high among rare cervical adenocarcinoma subtypes. Mucinous variants had significantly better overall survival than non-mucinous subtypes. These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the retrospective, single-center design and small number of human papillomavirus-negative cases, which limited statistical power for survival comparisons.

title: Age-specific HPV genotype distribution and associations with cervical lesions and vaginal microecological status in Northeast China: a retrospective study of 73,828 individuals
abstract: Background Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) infection is a major etiological factor in cervical carcinogenesis. HPV prevalence and genotype distribution show substantial geographic heterogeneity across China, highlighting the need for region-specific epidemiological data. This study characterized age-specific HPV infection and genotype patterns in Northeast China and further examined their associations with cervical pathology and vaginal microecological status. Methods We retrospectively analyzed HPV genotyping data from 73,828 individuals tested between 2020 and 2024. Histopathological data were available for 8,755 women, and vaginal microecological assessments were available for 2,428 women. Age-related differences, HPV genotype distributions, infection patterns, and their associations with cervical pathology and vaginal microecological categories were evaluated using nonparametric and χ2 tests. Results Overall HPV positivity was 20.83% (15,376/73,828) and showed a bimodal age distribution, with the highest prevalence among participants aged < 25 years (34.44%) and a second peak at 60–65 years (25.90%). HPV16, HPV52, and HPV58 were the three most frequently detected genotypes. Single HR-HPV infection differed significantly across cervical histopathological categories and was most frequent in cervical cancer (57.81%, P < 0.001). HPV positivity also differed across vaginal microecological categories ( P < 0.001), with the highest rate observed in the bacterial vaginosis group (32.66%); however, no individual HPV genotype remained significantly associated with microecological category after FDR correction. Conclusion These findings provide regional epidemiological evidence for HPV surveillance and cervical cancer prevention planning and support further prospective investigation of the relationship between vaginal microecological alterations and HPV infection.
journal: Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology

title: The Impact of Intratumoral Bacterial Response to Vaccine Therapy in Cancer Treatment
abstract: Therapeutic Human papillomavirus (HPVs) vaccines are designed to enhance the immunogenicity of HPV and promote the elimination of tumor cells effectively. Mounting evidence implies that tumor-resident microbiomes may influence therapeutic outcomes through immune modulation. In this study, we evaluated whether the intratumoral microbiota affects the efficacy of the therapeutic HPV vaccine. We analyzed RNA sequencing data from tumor tissues of C57BL/6N female mice treated with a DNA vaccine incorporating HPV16 E6/E7 antigens fused with the chemokine CCL11. Microbial community data were acquired using the PathSeq bioinformatics pipeline. Alpha diversity was estimated using the Shannon index and the number of observed taxonomic features, while beta diversity was assessed via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis distance. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis was performed to identify differentially abundant microbial taxa. Immune cell infiltration was characterized using the xCell deconvolution method. The analysis revealed significant divergence in both the alpha- and beta-diversity metrics of intratumoral microbiota, associated with treatment responsiveness. Vaccinated groups exhibited enriched abundances of the phyla Proteobacteria, together with a concomitant reduction in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and were associated with a positive response to cancer immunotherapy. Additionally, intratumoral microbiome composition and diversity correlated with the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and myeloid cells. This study identifies intratumoral microbiota remodeling as a key feature of therapeutic HPV vaccine response. The observed coordination between bacterial signatures and immune cell infiltration is associative and raises the hypothesis that intratumoral bacteria may modulate, rather than drive, antitumor immunity. These findings support the development of intratumoral microbiota profiling and highlight the potential for microbiota-targeted strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy efficacy.

source_records.title: The Impact of Intratumoral Bacterial Response to Vaccine Therapy in Cancer Treatment
source_records.abstract: Therapeutic Human papillomavirus (HPVs) vaccines are designed to enhance the immunogenicity of HPV and promote the elimination of tumor cells effectively. Mounting evidence implies that tumor-resident microbiomes may influence therapeutic outcomes through immune modulation. In this study, we evaluated whether the intratumoral microbiota affects the efficacy of the therapeutic HPV vaccine. We analyzed RNA sequencing data from tumor tissues of C57BL/6N female mice treated with a DNA vaccine incorporating HPV16 E6/E7 antigens fused with the chemokine CCL11. Microbial community data were acquired using the PathSeq bioinformatics pipeline. Alpha diversity was estimated using the Shannon index and the number of observed taxonomic features, while beta diversity was assessed via principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) based on Bray–Curtis distance. Linear discriminant analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) analysis was performed to identify differentially abundant microbial taxa. Immune cell infiltration was characterized using the xCell deconvolution method. The analysis revealed significant divergence in both the alpha- and beta-diversity metrics of intratumoral microbiota, associated with treatment responsiveness. Vaccinated groups exhibited enriched abundances of the phyla Proteobacteria, together with a concomitant reduction in Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, and were associated with a positive response to cancer immunotherapy. Additionally, intratumoral microbiome composition and diversity correlated with the increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, natural killer T (NKT) cells, and myeloid cells. This study identifies intratumoral microbiota remodeling as a key feature of therapeutic HPV vaccine response. The observed coordination between bacterial signatures and immune cell infiltration is associative and raises the hypothesis that intratumoral bacteria may modulate, rather than drive, antitumor immunity. These findings support the development of intratumoral microbiota profiling and highlight the potential for microbiota-targeted strategies to enhance cancer immunotherapy efficacy.

title: Association of viral load values with cervical lesion severity and exploratory genotype analysis in HPV-positive Indian women
abstract: Background Hybrid Capture 2 (HC2) provides a semi-quantitative estimate of high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) burden as relative light units/cutoff (RLU/CO), and HPV genotyping may add value to triage assessment. We evaluated the association of RLU/CO with cervical lesion severity and explored whether genotype information improves diagnostic performance in HPV-positive Indian women. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted in two sequential phases. In the initial phase, 217 consecutive HPV-positive women underwent HC2 HPV DNA testing, colposcopy-guided biopsy, and histopathological assessment. In a subsequent phase, an additional group of 111 HPV-positive women underwent the same clinical and histopathological assessment and also provided specimens for HPV genotyping. The genotype-enriched group was analysed separately for genotype distribution, co-infection patterns, and exploratory genotype-integrated prediction models. Age, Histopathology, and viral load (HC2 RLU/CO) were analysed in the full cohort. The genotyped subset was additionally evaluated for HPV genotype distribution and genotype-integrated ROC models. Descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis testing with Holm-adjusted Dunn's post-hoc comparisons, and ROC analyses with 95% confidence intervals and paired DeLong comparisons were performed. Results RLU/CO values differed across study-specific histopathological severity categories, with higher median values in LSIL, HSIL, and invasive cervical cancer than in normal histology and chronic cervicitis. In the cohort of 328 women, RLU/CO discriminated HSIL or invasive cervical cancer (severity score ≥3) with an AUC of 0.798 (95% CI, 0.726–0.868). A study-derived Youden-index cutoff of 12.08 RLU/CO yielded a sensitivity of 81.1% (95% CI, 69.5%–90.9%) and specificity of 73.1% (95% CI, 68.0%–78.0%). Among 111 genotyped participants, HPV16 was the most frequently detected genotype, and multiple-genotype infections occurred in 64 participants (57.7%). In the genotyped subgroup, comparative ROC analysis for HSIL or invasive cervical cancer showed AUCs of 0.659 for RLU/CO alone, 0.608 for RLU/CO plus HPV16/18, and 0.461 for RLU/CO plus other high-risk HPV. Neither genotype-integrated model improved discrimination compared with RLU/CO alone; these exploratory estimates require validation in larger independent cohorts. Conclusion HC2 RLU/CO showed potential for identifying HSIL or invasive cervical cancer. The study-derived cutoff requires validation in independent populations. Genotype-integrated models showed variable performance in the small subgroup. The HPV16/18 model was comparable to RLU/CO alone, but findings were exploratory. Larger prospective studies are needed before clinical implementation.

title: EVALUATION OF SCREENING PROTOCOLS FOR GYNECOLOGIC ONCOLOGY IN PUBLIC HEALTH
abstract: Cervical cancer represents a significant public health problem, primarily associated with persistent infection with oncogenic human papillomavirus (HPV). Continuous screening is an essential preventive strategy for the early detection of precancerous lesions. However, significant challenges persist in Brazil due to low cytopathological coverage, regional disparities, and discontinuity in care. This study aimed to analyze the scientific evidence regarding cervical cancer screening methods and the barriers to their effective implementation in the Unified Health System (SUS). This is a narrative literature review conducted in the PubMed database using the search terms “Early Detection of Cancer” and “Genital Neoplasms, Female.” The findings reveal an excess of tests performed outside the recommended age range, significant socioeconomic barriers, and limited access to confirmatory diagnosis and treatment. Molecular HPV DNA tests have high potential to improve primary screening, although their incorporation requires a substantial expansion of healthcare capacity and the support network. It is concluded that the effectiveness of early detection depends on the consolidation of an organized screening model, addressing inequities in access, and ensuring a comprehensive continuum of care for women.

title: An Integrated Approach to Cervical Cancer Prevention Based on WHO’s 90-70-90 Targets: A Rural Community-Based Study
abstract: BackgroundCervical cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in women, mainly affecting women in lowand middle-income countries.The present study aimed to raise awareness about cervical cancer among rural populations in Haryana, India, and provide cervical cancer screening for women and vaccination for girls and young women. MethodologyThis community-based cross-sectional study included three distinct study populations targeted for different interventions, i.e., cervical cancer awareness, cervical cancer screening, and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination initiatives.Awareness was delivered through community health camps, interactive sessions, street plays (nukkad natak), and the distribution of pamphlets.Cervical cancer screening was conducted through HPV DNA detection using multiplex PCR.Furthermore, eligible girls and young women were provided with the CERVAVAC HPV vaccine (Serum Institute of India Pvt. ResultsAwareness campaigns were conducted among the rural population of Haryana to provide knowledge about cervical cancer and its prevention.A total of 1,180 women aged over 18 years who attended the awareness campaigns (n = 1,000) and cervical cancer screening (n = 700) were briefly interviewed.Of these, 13.8% had heard of cervical cancer, 9.2% had poor knowledge about it, and 9% knew that the disease could be prevented.The HPV DNA positivity rate was 8.4% (59/700), with high-risk HPV genotypes (other than HPV-16 and HPV-18) being the most commonly detected, followed by HPV-18 (20%) and HPV-16 (10%), while 7% were co-infected with HPV-16 and HPV-18.A total of 102 individuals, comprising 17 (16.7%)girls aged 9-14 years and 85 (83.3%) girls/women aged 15-26 years, received HPV vaccination.Vaccine hesitancy was observed among the eligible population, with misinformation on social media cited as one of the reasons. ConclusionOur findings underscore the need for community-based cervical cancer awareness campaigns, strengthening health education from the school level, and providing access to HPV screening and vaccination facilities to improve cervical cancer prevention in rural settings.

title: Anal HSIL and Anal Cancer Outcomes Among non-HIV Immunosuppressed Patients: A Scoping Review
abstract: Background: Anal squamous cell carcinoma (ASCC) and its precursor lesion, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), are strongly associated with persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Non-HIV immunosuppressed patients such as solid organ transplant recipients, patients with hematologic malignancies, and individuals receiving immunosuppressive therapy for autoimmune conditions face an increased risk for anal HSIL and ASCC, along with higher recurrence rates and worse overall prognosis. Given the inherent heterogeneity of this population and its dispersal across multiple clinical specialties, randomized controlled trials on anal HSIL and ASCC treatment outcomes are unlikely to ever be available to guide clinical decision-making in these patients. Aim: This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature on treatment outcomes of HSIL and anal cancer in non-HIV immunosuppressed patients. Specifically, we seek to characterize the breadth and heterogeneity of available evidence on treatment response, recurrence, disease progression, survival, and adverse events; to identify gaps in outcome reporting and limitations in existing studies. These data will inform the development of a framework for standardized outcome reporting in future studies of these populations. Methods: we will conduct a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane without date restrictions. We will include all study designs, and studies will be eligible if they report on non-HIV immunosuppressed patients diagnosed with anal HSIL or ASCC, regardless of clinical setting. Studies focused exclusively on HIV-positive patients, immunocompetent populations, or reporting only cancer incidence without outcome data will be excluded, as will animal studies and conference abstracts without available full text. Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review. Data extraction will be performed by one reviewer and verified by a second reviewer or the senior author. Results will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Expected Outcomes: This review is expected to produce a comprehensive map of the existing evidence on treatment outcomes of HSIL and anal cancer in non-HIV immunosuppressed patients. By identifying critical gaps in knowledge and heterogeneity in outcome reporting, we aim to provide a foundation for future primary research and to propose a standardized framework for outcome reporting in this understudied population. Ultimately, this work aims to inform clinical decision-making and support the development of evidence-based guidelines for a vulnerable patient group largely underrepresented in the existing literature.

title: Microbial Oncology: A Critical Appraisal of Microbe-associated Carcinogenesis from Established Infectious Causes to the Contested Tumour Microbiome
abstract: Infectious agents remain among the few modifiable causes of human cancer for which prevention has already altered population-level incidence, yet the intellectual boundaries of the field have shifted substantially. Classical infectious carcinogenesis, built on a small set of viruses, bacteria and parasites with documented aetiological roles, now coexists with a far broader proposition that resident microbial communities within tumours and at distant mucosal sites shape tumour initiation, progression and treatment response. This review examines how securely that broader proposition is supported, and where the evidence remains provisional. Literature was identified through structured searching of biomedical and multidisciplinary scholarly sources, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking and by targeted retrieval of corrections and retractions, with appraisal focused on study design, biological specificity, contamination control, replication and the distance between mechanistic plausibility and demonstrated clinical effect. Several conclusions are well supported: oncogenic viruses operate largely through sustained expression of viral oncoproteins and genomic integration; Helicobacter pylori eradication reduces gastric cancer incidence, although the absolute benefit depends strongly on baseline risk and mucosal stage at treatment; and vaccination against hepatitis B virus and human papillomavirus has produced measurable declines in attributable malignancy. Evidence for bacterial contributions to colorectal carcinogenesis is mechanistically rich but complicated by unresolved taxonomy, inconsistent detection thresholds and limited prospective data. The pan-cancer intratumoural microbiome literature has been materially destabilised by demonstrated analytical errors and a high-profile retraction, which narrowed rather than abolished the field's claims. Microbiota-based prediction of immunotherapy response replicates only partially across cohorts, and randomised faecal microbiota transplantation evidence remains small and early phase. The central unresolved problems concern causal attribution in low-biomass settings, strain-level rather than genus-level resolution, and the near-absence of prospective interventional designs capable of distinguishing microbial drivers from microbial consequences of established tumours. Progress will depend less on additional descriptive surveys than on contamination-controlled, strain-resolved and prospectively designed studies.

title: LEEP excision depth is not independently associated with margin positivity or recorded postoperative hrHPV positivity in women with CIN2/3: a retrospective cohort study
abstract: Objective To examine the relationship between loop electrosurgical excision procedure (LEEP) excision depth and both margin status and postoperative high-risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) positivity in women treated for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grades 2–3 (CIN2/3), and to identify clinical factors associated with these outcomes. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study using deidentified institutional clinical and pathology records from Hainan General Hospital (Hainan Affiliated Hospital of Hainan Medical University). Pathology-recorded LEEP excision depth was evaluated as a continuous variable per 3-mm increment. The primary outcome was positive versus negative excision margin status, and the secondary outcome was recorded postoperative hrHPV positivity. Multivariable logistic regression models were adjusted for age, CIN grade, and preoperative HPV16/18 status. The robustness of the findings was further examined using nonlinear modeling, alternative margin definitions, inverse-probability-of-observation weighting, and interaction analyses. Because postoperative hrHPV testing was non-standardized and outcome data were substantially incomplete, these limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of the present retrospective investigation. title: Correlation of p16 Protein Status With MicroRNA Expression in Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Mobile Tongue: A Pilot Study
abstract: BackgroundThe role of p16 as a surrogate marker for human papillomavirus (HPV) infection in pure mobile-tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) remains controversial, and potential associations between p16 status and microRNA (miRNA) expression profiles are largely unexplored. ObjectiveThe objective of this study was to perform a pilot, hypothesis-generating correlative analysis of p16 protein expression (used here strictly as a surrogate marker, without direct HPV testing) and pre-existing miRNA data in an archival cohort of mobile-TSCCs, with the aim of nominating candidate miRNAs for future validation rather than identifying a definitive miRNA signature. MethodsPaired tumor and adjacent non-neoplastic specimens from 12 consecutive patients with primary mobile-TSCC who underwent surgical resection between 2010 and 2011 were previously profiled for mature miRNA expression.After exclusion of one sample for failure of the original quality-control criterion and one further case with incomplete p16 or miRNA data, a final matched cohort of 10 patients was analyzed.p16 immunohistochemistry was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor sections; positivity was defined as moderate-to-intense nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in ≥70% of neoplastic cells.Associations between tumor miRNA cycle-threshold values (84 mature human miRNAs) and p16 status, as well as other clinicopathological variables, were examined with non-parametric tests and Benjamini-Hochberg falsediscovery-rate (FDR) correction. ResultsTwo of the 10 tumors (20%) were classified as p16-positive.Twelve miRNAs exhibited nominal differences between p16-positive and p16-negative tumors (uncorrected Mann-Whitney p = 0.044 for all 12); none remained statistically significant after FDR correction (all FDR ≥ 0.31).The most pronounced numerical elevations in the p16-positive subset were observed for miR-150-5p (approximate fold-change 9.6), miR-206 (6.9), miR-155-5p (4.9), miR-146a-5p (4.0) and miR-29b-3p (3.8).No robust associations were identified with patient outcome, sex, T-stage, histological differentiation, tumor side, hospital of origin, or age.The study was not powered to detect moderate effect sizes and all analyses are exploratory. ConclusionsIn this small pilot cohort, p16 status showed only nominal, non-FDR-significant differences in miRNA expression.The numerical elevation of the established oncomiR miR-155-5p in the two p16-positive tumors is hypothesis-generating but requires confirmation in larger multi-institutional series that incorporate both rigorous p16 assessment and direct HPV molecular testing.

ObjectiveThe objective of this study was to perform a pilot, hypothesis-generating correlative analysis of p16 protein expression (used here strictly as a surrogate marker, without direct HPV testing) and pre-existing miRNA data in an archival cohort of mobile-TSCCs, with the aim of nominating candidate miRNAs for future validation rather than identifying a definitive miRNA signature. MethodsPaired tumor and adjacent non-neoplastic specimens from 12 consecutive patients with primary mobile-TSCC who underwent surgical resection between 2010 and 2011 were previously profiled for mature miRNA expression.After exclusion of one sample for failure of the original quality-control criterion and one further case with incomplete p16 or miRNA data, a final matched cohort of 10 patients was analyzed.p16 immunohistochemistry was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor sections; positivity was defined as moderate-to-intense nuclear and cytoplasmic staining in ≥70% of neoplastic cells.Associations between tumor miRNA cycle-threshold values (84 mature human miRNAs) and p16 status, as well as other clinicopathological variables, were examined with non-parametric tests and Benjamini-Hochberg falsediscovery-rate (FDR) correction. ResultsTwo of the 10 tumors (20%) were classified as p16-positive.Twelve miRNAs exhibited nominal differences between p16-positive and p16-negative tumors (uncorrected Mann-Whitney p = 0.044 for all 12); none remained statistically significant after FDR correction (all FDR ≥ 0.31).The most pronounced numerical elevations in the p16-positive subset were observed for miR-150-5p (approximate fold-change 9.6), miR-206 (6.9), miR-155-5p (4.9), miR-146a-5p (4.0) and miR-29b-3p (3.8).No robust associations were identified with patient outcome, sex, T-stage, histological differentiation, tumor side, hospital of origin, or age.The study was not powered to detect moderate effect sizes and all analyses are exploratory. ConclusionsIn this small pilot cohort, p16 status showed only nominal, non-FDR-significant differences in miRNA expression.The numerical elevation of the established oncomiR miR-155-5p in the two p16-positive tumors is hypothesis-generating but requires confirmation in larger multi-institutional series that incorporate both rigorous p16 assessment and direct HPV molecular testing.

title: Awareness of Cervical Cancer Screening Among Women Attending Gynecology Clinics
abstract: Background: Cervical cancer is preventable and can be detected early with screening, which can help to lower the morbidity and mortality from the disease. The purpose of this study was to determine the awareness of women's screening for cervical cancer in gynecology clinics. Methods: This cross-sectional descriptive study included 175 women attending gynecology clinics. A structured interviewer-administered questionnaire was used to collect data, which included information on cervical cancer prevention, Pap smear testing, HPV infection testing, screening without symptoms, previous gynecological consultation, and sources of information about screening. A score of awareness was computed, and participants were divided into good, moderate, or poor awareness. Relationships with sociodemographic and health-care related factors were explored. Results: In general, 103(58.9%) of women were aware, and 72(41.1%) were not aware. Of the 121 respondents (69.1%) who recognized Pap smear as a screening test, 68 (38.9%) knew that HPV testing could be used for screening, and 83 (47.4%) knew that screening might be recommended when there are no symptoms. There was a significant increase in awareness, from 32.3% for women with primary education or less to 83.3% for women with graduate education (p<0.001). Conclusion: Awareness was moderate, with key gaps in knowledge around HPV-based screening and symptom-independent screening. Clinic-based education and subsequent intervention studies should reinforce informed participation in screening, particularly among women who have not been extensively educated or provided with information.

title: An in vitro analysis of Fusobacterium nucleatum infection on oral squamous cell carcinoma
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) represents a significant global health burden, with incidence increasing while five-year survival has remained largely unchanged for decades. Although tobacco, alcohol and human papillomavirus are established risk factors, an increasing proportion of cases occur in patients lacking these traditional exposures, highlighting the potential contribution of the oral microbiome. Fusobacterium nucleatum, an oral anaerobe with an established carcinogenic role in colorectal cancer, has been detected in OSCC tissue; however, its contribution to OSCC progression remains poorly characterised. This study investigated the effects and underlying mechanisms of F. nucleatum infection in OSCC using a three-dimensional SCC-4 spheroid model designed to recapitulate key features of the tumour microenvironment, including hypoxia. Spheroid hypoxia was validated using HIF-1α western blotting and immunofluorescence staining, while intracellular bacterial localisation was confirmed by immunofluorescence and antibiotic protection assays. Bulk RNA sequencing identified activation of the NF-κB signalling pathway following F. nucleatum infection, consistent with an infection-associated inflammatory response. Furthermore, specific antagonist treatment confirmed these findings. Collectively, these results provide mechanistic evidence linking F. nucleatum infection to NF-κB-driven inflammatory signalling in OSCC. The pharmacological reversibility of this phenotype by a specific antagonist suggests the possibility of novel therapeutic strategies for infection-associated OSCC and supports a functional role for the oral microbiome in OSCC pathogenesis. Further in vivo studies are warranted to validate these findings and investigate whether tumour infection status could inform response to IAP-targeted therapies.

title: Knowledge Regarding Cervical Cancer and Factors Associated with it Among Women of Reproductive Age Group of Butwal Sub-Metropolitan City, Rupandehi, Nepal
abstract: Background: Cervical cancer is largely preventable through human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination, screening, and timely management of precancerous lesions. Adequate knowledge among women of reproductive age is important for the uptake of preventive services. To the best of our knowledge this is the first study of its kind conducted in Butwal Sub-Metropolitan City, Rupandehi, Nepal. Objective: To assess the knowledge and factors associated about cervical cancer among women of reproductive age group 15-49 years. Methods: A community-based descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted from October 2023 to March 2024 among women aged 15–49 years. Three wards (4, 8, and 11) were selected by lottery, followed by proportional allocation and systematic random sampling of the households. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using semi-structured questionnaires. Knowledge scores were not normally distributed; a median score of 7 was used to classify adequate (≥7) and inadequate (<7) knowledge. Descriptive statistics and chi-square test were performed. Results: Among 249 women, 45.4% respondents had adequate knowledge of cervical cancer while 54.6% had inadequate knowledge. Only 33.7% identified a virus as a cause of cervical cancer, while 14.0% identified HPV infection as a risk factor. Regular screening (60.6%) was the most frequently reported preventive measure. Although 68.7% had heard of HPV vaccination, 43.0% did not know the recommended age group and 39.0% did not know its availability. Conclusion: More than half of the women had inadequate knowledge of cervical cancer, highlighting the need for health education on HPV infection, vaccination and cervical cancer screening.

title: DIAGNOSTIC EFFICACY OF EXTENDED COLPOSCOPY IN THE EARLY DETECTION OF PRECANCEROUS LESIONS AND CERVICAL CANCER
abstract: Cervical cancer remains one of the major challenges in modern gynecologic oncology. Timely detection of precancerous lesions and early-stage malignant disease can improve treatment effectiveness and patient prognosis. Extended colposcopy is an important diagnostic method for identifying pathological changes in the cervix. It enables visualization of suspicious epithelial areas and helps determine the optimal site for a targeted biopsy. To evaluate the diagnostic efficacy of extended colposcopy in detecting high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cervical cancer. Materials and Methods. A comparative study model involving 100 women aged 25–65 years is presented. Group I consisted of 50 patients with benign cervical conditions, while Group II included 50 patients with histologically confirmed high-grade precancerous lesions or cervical cancer. The diagnostic evaluation included cervical cytology, extended colposcopy, and colposcopy-directed biopsy followed by histopathological examination. Based on hypothetical data, differences in colposcopic findings between the two groups were demonstrated, along with an illustrative calculation of the diagnostic sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of the method. Extended colposcopy is an important diagnostic method that facilitates the identification of suspicious epithelial areas and improves the diagnostic value of targeted biopsy. Definitive diagnosis is based on histopathological examination.

title: Desafios e diretrizes no atendimento ginecológico de mulheres muçulmanas com suspeita de câncer de colo do útero no Sistema Único de Saúde do Brasil: uma abordagem intercultural e de combate à violência institucional
abstract: This manuscript analyzes the challenges in gynecological care for Muslim women with suspected cervical cancer within the scope of the Unified Health System (SUS), proposing the incorporation of intercultural practices and procedures successful in international experience. Through a narrative review of national and international scientific literature, sociocultural, religious, linguistic, and institutional barriers that distance these users from conventional cytopathological screening are identified, resulting in late diagnoses and worse oncological prognosis. The study highlights how the inflexible imposition of invasive examinations by male professionals without adequate privacy constitutes a subtle form of gynecological and institutional violence. As practical proposals integrated into the doctrinal and operational principles of SUS, key highlights include flexible scheduling with guaranteed care exclusively by female professionals; the architectural and visual adaptation of examination rooms using screens and modesty garments; the preparation of translated and culturally sensitive educational materials demystifying Human Papillomavirus (HPV) and preserving the social value of the hymen in virgin women; the strategic involvement of cultural mediators and ethnic community health workers; the introduction of molecular self-sampling for HPV detection as a highly resolutive and minimally invasive alternative; and the implementation of multilingual telehealth with personalized navigation for onco-gynecological patients. The transposition of these international innovations modernizes Primary Health Care, ensuring effective cervical screening, preventing institutional violence, and reaffirming human dignity and equity within the Brazilian public health system.

title: Definition of joint biomarker signatures for patients with locally advanced HNSCC treated by postoperative radiochemotherapy – A multicentre study of the DKTK-ROG
abstract: Several prognostic biomarkers have previously been identified for patients with locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) treated with postoperative radiochemotherapy (PORT-C) in a comprehensive biomarker program conducted by the German Cancer Consortium - Radiation Oncology Group (DKTK-ROG). Here, we combined these biomarkers into composite signatures for loco-regional control (LRC) and overall survival (OS) in 143 patients with HPV16 DNA-negative tumours. The C-indices for baseline, extended and data-driven signatures were 0.77, 0.93 and 0.94 for LRC and 0.69, 0.83 and 0.82 for OS, respectively. These predefined models will next be tested in the prospective HNprädBio validation cohort, which has completed recruitment and data collection.

title: Reproductive health research and innovation in Sri Lanka: Challenges and the road ahead
abstract: Sri Lanka has achieved maternal and child health outcomes well above its income level, yet several reproductive health indicators have stalled or worsened. The prevalence of anaemia in pregnancy, for example, rose from 31.9% in 2009 to 35.4% in 2016. Since a national priority-setting exercise in 2007, research output on reproductive health has grown, but much of the local evidence has not been translated into practice.This article draws on two decades of work by a multidisciplinary team at the University of Peradeniya and Teaching Hospital Peradeniya. It summarises studies on maternal infections (varicella zoster, Toxoplasma gondii, human papillomavirus and group B streptococcus), metabolic disease in women, diabetes in pregnancy, the quality of intrapartum care, reproductive toxicology, and two medical devices developed with engineers: an automated urine volume monitor (patented) and an accelerometer-based fetal movement monitor (patent pending).The recurring barriers were the absence of national coordination and dedicated funding, fragmented research and data systems, slow policy translation, little work on environmental exposures, and limited time and supervision capacity. We propose a national reproductive health research registry and data repository, a National Reproductive Health Research and Innovation Council, a digital antenatal record, a training pipeline for clinician-scientists, investment in translational infrastructure, and incentives for interdisciplinary and international collaboration.
journal: Sri Lanka Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology

title: High Risk Latinas Awareness and Interest in Self-collection for HPV Testing to Prevent Cervical Cancer
abstract: Abstract: Introduction. Self-collection for human papilloma virus (HPV) testing can revolutionize the cervical cancer prevention landscape. However, dissemination of new tools can exacerbate existing inequities. This paper investigates awareness and interest in self-collection among a high-risk Latina population. Semi-structured interviews with middle-aged to older high-risk Latinas covered their awareness of and interest in using self-collection. The interviews were conducted as part of a larger study on cervical cancer. Twenty-six Latinas age 35 years or older diagnosed with pre-cervical cancer from the Pacific Northwest took part. We found mixed results in responses to interest in self-collection. Twelve would not do the self-collection; the 12 were a mix of English- and Spanish-speaking and U.S.-born, legal permanent residents or undocumented Latinas. All five participants who were conditional yes's were Spanish-speaking. Three sub-categories explain lack of interest or hesitancy. Dissemination efforts should have more hands-on demonstration and technical training, particularly for Spanish-speaking immigrant Latinx communities.
journal: Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved
