title: Factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women living in urban Nepal
abstract: Cervical cancer stigma can affect perceptions of cancer, interactions with affected people, and engagement in preventive behavior. Evidence on factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal is limited. This study examined sociodemographic, reproductive and knowledge-related factors associated with cervical cancer stigma. We analysed baseline data from 310 women aged 30 to 60 years enrolled in a community-based, two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial in Budanilkantha Municipality, Kathmandu, Nepal, between 15 June and 15 December 2022. Cervical cancer stigma was assessed using the validated Nepali version of the Cancer Stigma Scale. Multivariable generalized estimating equations (GEE) with a Gaussian distribution and identity link were used to examine associations, adjusting for age, ethnicity, religion, education, occupation, and annual household income. Results are reported as beta coefficients ({beta}) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The mean age was 41.5 years, and 54.2% of participants were Janjati. Overall, 82.3% had heard of cervical cancer, 31.8% knew its signs and symptoms, and 1.6% had heard of Human Papilloma Virus. Most knew cervical cancer could be prevented (75.6%) and treated (90.1%). After adjustment, Janjati women ({beta} = 0.311, 95% CI: 0.099, 0.523) and women from other ethnic groups, including Dalit and Madhesi ({beta} = 0.411, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.768), had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than Brahmin/Chettri women. Formal education was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores ({beta} = -0.359, 95% CI: -0.554, -0.165). Homemakers ({beta} = 0.263, 95% CI: 0.014, 0.513) and self-employed women ({beta} = 0.309, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.564) had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than salaried women. Awareness of cervical cancer ({beta} = -0.249, 95% CI: -0.437, -0.060), its signs and symptoms ({beta} = -0.245, 95% CI: -0.465, -0.025), preventability ({beta} = -0.285, 95% CI: -0.554, -0.016) and treatability ({beta} = -0.362, 95% CI: -0.635, -0.089) was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores. Age, religion, income, risk-factor awareness, menopause history, number of pregnancies and use of Intra Uterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCD) use were not significantly associated with cervical cancer stigma. Cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal was associated with educational status, ethnicity, employment, and specific aspects of cervical cancer knowledge. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether improving cancer knowledge can effectively reduce cervical cancer stigma.

source_records.title: Factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women living in urban Nepal
source_records.abstract: Cervical cancer stigma can affect perceptions of cancer, interactions with affected people, and engagement in preventive behavior. Evidence on factors associated with cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal is limited. This study examined sociodemographic, reproductive and knowledge-related factors associated with cervical cancer stigma. We analysed baseline data from 310 women aged 30 to 60 years enrolled in a community-based, two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial in Budanilkantha Municipality, Kathmandu, Nepal, between 15 June and 15 December 2022. Cervical cancer stigma was assessed using the validated Nepali version of the Cancer Stigma Scale. Multivariable generalized estimating equations (GEE) with a Gaussian distribution and identity link were used to examine associations, adjusting for age, ethnicity, religion, education, occupation, and annual household income. Results are reported as beta coefficients ({beta}) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The mean age was 41.5 years, and 54.2% of participants were Janjati. Overall, 82.3% had heard of cervical cancer, 31.8% knew its signs and symptoms, and 1.6% had heard of Human Papilloma Virus. Most knew cervical cancer could be prevented (75.6%) and treated (90.1%). After adjustment, Janjati women ({beta} = 0.311, 95% CI: 0.099, 0.523) and women from other ethnic groups, including Dalit and Madhesi ({beta} = 0.411, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.768), had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than Brahmin/Chettri women. Formal education was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores ({beta} = -0.359, 95% CI: -0.554, -0.165). Homemakers ({beta} = 0.263, 95% CI: 0.014, 0.513) and self-employed women ({beta} = 0.309, 95% CI: 0.054, 0.564) had higher cervical cancer stigma scores than salaried women. Awareness of cervical cancer ({beta} = -0.249, 95% CI: -0.437, -0.060), its signs and symptoms ({beta} = -0.245, 95% CI: -0.465, -0.025), preventability ({beta} = -0.285, 95% CI: -0.554, -0.016) and treatability ({beta} = -0.362, 95% CI: -0.635, -0.089) was associated with lower cervical cancer stigma scores. Age, religion, income, risk-factor awareness, menopause history, number of pregnancies and use of Intra Uterine Contraceptive Devices (IUCD) use were not significantly associated with cervical cancer stigma. Cervical cancer stigma among women in urban Nepal was associated with educational status, ethnicity, employment, and specific aspects of cervical cancer knowledge. Longitudinal and intervention studies are needed to determine whether improving cancer knowledge can effectively reduce cervical cancer stigma.

full_text: Correction: Japanese-Language AI Agent System for Human Papillomavirus Vaccine Infoveillance and Public Communication: Development and Feasibility Evaluation In “Japanese-Language AI Agent System for Human Papillomavirus Vaccine Infoveillance and Public Communication: Development and Feasibility Evaluation”, we identified several items requiring correction. They are set out below in the order in which they appear in the article, providing the original published text and the corrected text. None of the corrections change any finding or conclusion of the article. First, in the author byline, the degree designations of three authors were incorrect. The byline originally read: Junyu Liu, PhD; Siwen Yang, BEng; Dexiu Ma, PhD; Qian Niu, PhD; Zequn Zhang, PhD; Momoko Nagai-Tanima, PhD; Tomoki Aoyama, MD, PhD The corrected byline now reads: Junyu Liu, ME; Siwen Yang, BEng; Dexiu Ma, MS; Qian Niu, PhD; Zequn Zhang, MS; Momoko Nagai-Tanima, PhD; Tomoki Aoyama, MD, PhD Second, in the section Report Generation Evaluation Methodology in the Methods section, the following text was corrected: Both protocols use LLM-based judges with standardized scoring rubrics, generating scores on a scale from 0 to 5 (Multimedia Appendices 4 and 5) for each dimension. The text now reads: Both protocols were applied by 3 domain experts using the standardized scoring rubrics provided in Multimedia Appendices 4 and 5, assigning scores on a scale from 0 to 5 for each dimension. Each expert scored every report section independently. This aligns the paragraph with the remainder of the same section (“Three volunteers read and scored each report independently”) and with the Results section (“Three evaluators independently scored each report section”), which are correct. The values reported in Table 5 and Multimedia Appendix 10 (included here as Multimedia Appendix 1) are the scores of these 3 raters. An automated large language model–based checker was also implemented and executed, but its output was not used for the values reported in this article. This correction does not affect the corresponding sentence in the section Chatbot Evaluation Methodology, where the chatbot evaluation was indeed performed by large language model–based judges, as stated. Third, in the Social Media Analysis subsection of the Methods, the stance classifier assigns one of three labels; no “unclear” label is produced. The sentence, which read: Stance classification categorizes each post as supportive, opposed, neutral, or unclear regarding HPV vaccination using batch LLM inference with a temporal context, thereby aggregating daily counts to track sentiment evolution. has been corrected to: Stance classification categorizes each post as supportive, opposed, or neutral regarding HPV vaccination using batch LLM inference with a temporal context, thereby aggregating daily counts to track sentiment evolution. The daily counts reported in the article were aggregated over the three labels the classifier assigns, so no reported value changes. In the same section, misinformation detection flags a post and records a short statement of the claim; it does not assign the post to a type. The sentence, which read: Misinformation detection uses LLM-based analysis to identify posts containing claims that contradict the established scientific consensus, categorizing detected content by type (safety concerns, efficacy doubts, and conspiracy theories) for institutional awareness. has been corrected to: Misinformation detection uses LLM-based analysis to identify posts containing claims that contradict the established scientific consensus, recording for each flagged post a short statement of the claim for institutional awareness. No counts by type are reported in the article, so no reported value changes. Fourth, the row for chat conversations in Table 1 described the set of conversations used for the chatbot evaluation, but the three values in the row were derived from three different populations. The row was published as: Collection Documents (n=139,803), n (%) Unique source Primary language Chat conversations 139 (0.10) 31 sessions Japanese (59.3%) The table row has been corrected to the following: Collection Documents (n=139,803), n (%) Unique source Primary language Chat conversations 139 (0.10) 37 sessions English (98.6%); Japanese (1.4%) The following footnote has been added to Table 1: The chat row describes the conversation set used for the chatbot evaluation: 139 turns, each stored as one document, from 37 conversations. Language proportions were computed over the 139 user messages in this set. Primary language for the Papers, Official documents and Social media rows was assigned on the basis of the source of each collection and was not derived from automated language detection. The other three rows of Table 1, the column percentages, and the total of 139,803 documents are unchanged. Specifically, the number of sessions has been corrected from 31 to 37. The 139 documents are the 139 single-turn question-answer exchanges reported in Table 2, which originate from 37 conversations (Multimedia Appendix 6). The figure of 31 is the number of conversations used for the multiturn evaluation reported in Table 3 (Multimedia Appendix 7), which comprise 133 turns. The language proportions have been corrected. Computed over the 139 user messages in this set, 137 (98.6%) are in English and 2 (1.4%) are in Japanese. The previously reported value of “Japanese (59.3%)” was derived from a different population and does not describe the 139 documents referred to in this row. Fifth, the multiturn evaluation block of Table 4 was published as: Check type and dimension Rater 1 Rater 2 Rater 3 MADa Spearman ρ (95% CI) ICCb(3,1) (95% CI) Multiturn evaluation (n=11 conversations) Context memory 0.13 0.13 0.13 0.13 — 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) Topic centering 0 0.13 0 0.04 — 0.000 (−0.307 to 0.545) Identity 0 0.13 0.55 0.21 — 0.174 (−0.208 to 0.684) Table 4 has been corrected as follows: Check type and dimension Rater 1 Rater 2 Rater 3 MADa Spearman ρ (95% CI) ICCb(3,1) (95% CI) Multiturn evaluation (n=8 conversations) Context memory 0.13 0.13 0.13 0.13 — —e Topic centering 0 0.13 0 0.04 — 0.000 (−0.307 to 0.545) Identity 0 0.13 0.50 0.21 — 0.174 (−0.208 to 0.684) The new footnote e reads: e The 3 experts’ scores were all the same, and the ICC could not be calculated. All statistics in the multiturn block of Table 4 were computed over these 8 conversations; the header overstated the number. For the Context memory row, all 3 experts assigned a score of 5 to every conversation, so the between-item variance is zero and the intraclass correlation coefficient is undefined; the em dash follows the convention already used in the Spearman ρ column of the same table. The single-turn evaluation block of Table 4 is unchanged. Sixth, in the Results section, the following text was revised: n=20 for single-turn evaluation and n=11 for multiturn evaluation The text has been corrected to: n=20 question-answer pairs for single-turn evaluation and n=8 conversations for multiturn evaluation The corrected text also names the unit of each evaluation set. Seventh, in the Results section, the following sentence was corrected: Context memory showed perfect interrater reliability (ICC=1.000) as all 3 experts assigned identical scores, whereas topic centering (ICC=0.000) and identity (ICC=0.174) showed that the small deviations among raters did not follow consistent patterns—a consequence of near-ceiling score distributions. The text now reads: All 3 experts assigned identical scores to every conversation for context memory, whereas topic centering (ICC=0.000) and identity (ICC=0.174) showed that the small deviations among raters did not follow consistent patterns—a consequence of near-ceiling score distributions. This aligns the sentence with the correction to the ICC(3,1) column in item 5. Eighth, in the section Report Generation in the Results, the following text was corrected: Citation correctness was the most variable dimension (median 4.00, IQR 4.00‐5.00; mean 4.21, 95% CI 3.96‐4.46), with scores spanning the range of 4 to 5 The text now reads: Citation correctness was the most variable dimension (median 4.00, IQR 4.00‐5.00; mean 4.21, 95% CI 3.96‐4.46), with scores spanning the range of 3 to 5 Ninth, in Table 5, the rows for Helpfulness and Citation correctness originally read: Dimension Score (0‐5), mean (SD; 95% CI) Score (0‐5), median (IQR) Score of 5, % Score of ≥4, % Score of ≤3, % Helpfulness 4.12 (3.98‐4.27) 4.00 (4.00‐4.00) 19 94 0 Citation correctness 4.21 (3.96‐4.46) 4.00 (4.00‐5.00) 29 92 0 The rows have been corrected to the following: Dimension Score (0‐5), mean (SD; 95% CI) Score (0‐5), median (IQR) Score of 5, % Score of ≥4, % Score of ≤3, % Helpfulness 4.12 (3.98‐4.27) 4.00 (4.00‐4.00) 19 94 6 Citation correctness 4.21 (3.96‐4.46) 4.00 (4.00‐5.00) 29 92 8 The published values in the “Score of ≤3, %” column were inconsistent with the “Score of ≥4, %” column in the same rows. The corrected values correspond to 3 of the 48 helpfulness scores and 2 of the 24 citation correctness scores being 3 (3/48, 6%; 2/24, 8%). The other three rows of Table 5 are unchanged. Tenth, in the section Interpretation in the Discussion, the following sentence has been deleted: The higher agreement in multiturn evaluation, where full dialogue context is available (context memory ICC=1.000), supports this interpretation. Eleventh, in the section Limitations in the Discussion, the following text was revised: The evaluation dataset (31 conversations and 139 exchanges) may not capture all real-world interaction patterns This has been corrected to the following: The evaluation datasets (139 single-turn exchanges and 31 multiturn conversations) may not capture all real-world interaction patterns The two figures in the original text described different evaluation sets: the 139 exchanges are the single-turn evaluation items (Multimedia Appendix 6), whereas the 31 conversations are the multiturn evaluation set (Multimedia Appendix 7), which comprises 133 turns. As printed, the two figures could be read as the conversation and turn counts of a single set. Twelfth, in the Conclusions section of the Discussion, the following text was revised: The integrated architecture may enable bidirectional information flow—providing verified information with transparent source attribution to users while generating analytical reports for institutional stakeholders—creating feedback loops between public concerns and communication strategies. The text has been corrected to: The integrated architecture may enable bidirectional information flow—providing verified information with transparent source attribution to users while generating analytical reports for institutional stakeholders—creating links between public concerns and communication strategies. Only the term “feedback loops” has been changed. The term was used to refer to the circulation of information: conversations recorded with user consent become available to the report generation component so that public concerns can reach institutional readers. However, “feedback” also carries its control-theoretic sense, in which an output returns to the input and automatically adjusts the behavior of the system. The system implements no such loop: no path from the generated reports back to the conversational interface exists. Because the two senses can be confused, the term was not an appropriate choice. “Links” states the relationship without implying closure or automatic adjustment. No reported result is affected. Thirteenth, the authors have replaced Multimedia Appendix 10 (included here as Multimedia Appendix 1) with a new file. Three corrections have been made to it. In the table of reference evaluation results by section, the column headers “Completeness” and “Correctness” have been corrected to “Reference validity” and “Citation correctness,” respectively. The headers as published were those of the main text evaluation table above it; the columns contain reference validity and citation correctness scores. In the same table, the value for July 2020 / Paper / Citation correctness has been corrected from “4.00±0.00” to “4.00 ± 1.00.” The three expert scores for this cell were 3, 4, and 5. This is the only cell of that table whose value did not reproduce; the other 15 are unchanged. In the same table, the “Overall” values for Citation correctness have been corrected from “4.33±0.50” to “4.33±0.49” (News) and from “4.08±0.66” to “4.08±0.67” (Paper). The corresponding means are correct as published. The SDs in Multimedia Appendix 10 (included here as Multimedia Appendix 1) are sample SDs, consistent with the formulas in Multimedia Appendix 9 from which the table was produced. The following footnote has been added to both tables of the appendix file: Values are mean±sample standard deviation across the 3 evaluators, computed from the scores in Multimedia Appendix 9. The standard deviations reported in the Abstract are population standard deviations. None of these corrections affects the values reported in Table 5 or any finding of the study. Lastly, the Acknowledgments originally read: The authors used the generative artificial intelligence tool Claude [33] by Anthropic to refine the writing and structure of the manuscript, which was further reviewed and revised by the study group. The original Claude transcripts are available in Multimedia Appendix 11. This has been corrected to the following: The authors used the generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool Claude [33] by Anthropic to generate code, to assist with the analysis, to search the literature for references supporting statements in the manuscript, to retrieve reported figures from cited sources, and to refine the writing and structure of the manuscript. All AI-generated output was reviewed and revised by the study group. A record of part of these interactions is provided in Multimedia Appendix 11. The remaining interactions were not retained, so a complete transcript is not available. Two aspects of the original statement required correction. First, it described the use of the tool as limited to refining the writing and structure of the manuscript. The tool was in fact also used to generate code, to assist with the analysis, to search for literature supporting statements in the manuscript, and to retrieve figures from cited sources; the corrected text states this. Second, “the original Claude transcripts are available” could be read as indicating that the appendix contains the complete record. Multimedia Appendix 11 consists of 18 screenshots of part of these interactions; the remainder was not saved and cannot be supplied. The reported values do not depend on the correctness of any generated code: 280 reported values—those in Tables 1-5 and Multimedia Appendix 10 (included here as Multimedia Appendix 1), together with the associated statistics and bootstrap CIs reported in the text—have been independently recomputed from the saved evaluation data and the underlying document collections. Of these, 271 reproduce the values as published; the 9 that do not are precisely the numerical corrections in items 4, 5, 9, and 13 above. The CIs reproduce exactly under the random seed fixed in the analysis code. All coauthors have reviewed and approved these corrections and the replacement appendix file. We can provide their written agreement, a cell-level list of the changed appendix values, and the verification scripts and their output on request. The correction will appear in the online version of the paper on the JMIR Publications website together with the publication of this correction notice. Because this was made after submission to PubMed, PubMed Central, and other full-text repositories, the corrected article has also been resubmitted to those repositories. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Japanese-language AI agent system for HPV vaccine infoveillance and public communication, addressing the need for accurate and culturally relevant health information dissemination.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and feasibility evaluation of an AI agent system for HPV vaccine-related infoveillance, with data collected from chat conversations and social media posts in Japanese and English, involving 139,803 unique documents.
analysis.methods: The system used a large language model (LLM) for stance classification, with three raters evaluating interrater reliability using metrics such as MAD, Spearman ρ, and ICC. The evaluation included single-turn and multiturn conversations, with results based on statistical analysis of scores across different dimensions.
analysis.main_results: The study corrected several errors, including the number of conversations used for multiturn evaluation (from 11 to 8), the language distribution of chat documents (from 59.3% Japanese to 1.4% Japanese), and inconsistencies in the “Score of ≤3, %” column of Table 5. The ICC for context memory was 1.000, indicating perfect interrater reliability, while topic centering and identity showed lower reliability.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the feasibility of the AI agent system for HPV vaccine infoveillance, with the correction of errors enhancing the accuracy of reported results and reliability metrics.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of AI tools for HPV vaccine communication and public health surveillance, highlighting the importance of accurate data representation and reliability in health-related infoveillance systems.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results were based on corrected data, which may affect the interpretation of reliability metrics. The evidence is moderate due to the focus on feasibility and the limited scope of the corrections.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents a correction to a previous paper evaluating a Japanese-language AI agent system for HPV vaccine infoveillance and public communication. The corrections address errors in data reporting, including the number of conversations used for multiturn evaluation, language distribution of chat documents, and inconsistencies in score percentages. The study highlights the importance of accurate data representation and reliability in AI-based health communication tools. The findings suggest that the system is feasible for HPV vaccine-related infoveillance, with perfect interrater reliability for context memory but lower reliability for other dimensions. The evidence is moderate, as the corrections focus on data accuracy rather than comprehensive evaluation of the AI system's impact on public health outcomes. The study underscores the need for careful data handling in AI-driven health surveillance initiatives.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of a Japanese-language AI agent system for HPV vaccine infoveillance and public communication, addressing the need for accurate and culturally relevant health information dissemination.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved the development and feasibility evaluation of an AI agent system for HPV vaccine-related infoveillance, with data collected from chat conversations and social media posts in Japanese and English, involving 139,803 unique documents.
elements_en.methods: The system used a large language model (LLM) for stance classification, with three raters evaluating interrater reliability using metrics such as MAD, Spearman ρ, and ICC. The evaluation included single-turn and multiturn conversations, with results based on statistical analysis of scores across different dimensions.
elements_en.main_results: The study corrected several errors, including the number of conversations used for multiturn evaluation (from 11 to 8), the language distribution of chat documents (from 59.3% Japanese to 1.4% Japanese), and inconsistencies in the “Score of ≤3, %” column of Table 5. The ICC for context memory was 1.000, indicating perfect interrater reliability, while topic centering and identity showed lower reliability.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as demonstrating the feasibility of the AI agent system for HPV vaccine infoveillance, with the correction of errors enhancing the accuracy of reported results and reliability metrics.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the development of AI tools for HPV vaccine communication and public health surveillance, highlighting the importance of accurate data representation and reliability in health-related infoveillance systems.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results were based on corrected data, which may affect the interpretation of reliability metrics. The evidence is moderate due to the focus on feasibility and the limited scope of the corrections.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在评估日语人工智能代理系统用于 HPV 疫苗 信息监控和公共传播的可行性,满足准确且与文化相关的健康信息传播的需求。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及针对 HPV 疫苗 相关信息监视的人工智能代理系统的开发和可行性评估,数据从日语和英语的聊天对话和社交媒体帖子中收集,涉及 139,803 个独特文档。
elements_zh.methods: 该系统使用大型语言模型 (LLM) 进行立场分类,由三位评估者使用 MAD、Spearman ρ 和 ICC 等指标评估评估者之间的可靠性。评估包括单轮和多轮对话,结果基于不同维度分数的统计分析。
elements_zh.main_results: The study corrected several errors, including the number of conversations used for multiturn evaluation (from 11 to 8), the language distribution of chat documents (from 59.3% Japanese to 1.4% Japanese), and inconsistencies in the “Score of ≤3, %” column of Table 5. The ICC for context memory was 1.000, indicating perfect interrater reliability, while topic centering and identity showed lower reliability.
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为证明了用于 HPV 疫苗 信息监测的人工智能代理系统的可行性,错误的纠正提高了报告结果和可靠性指标的准确性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为 HPV 疫苗 通信和公共卫生 监测 的人工智能工具的开发提供了信息,强调了健康相关信息监控系统中准确数据表示和可靠性的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于校正数据,这可能会影响可靠性指标的解释。由于关注可行性和修正范围有限,证据是中等的。

full_text: Abstract To establish outcomes of Human Papillomavirus-Related Multiphenotypic Sinonasal Carcinoma and evaluate indications for adjuvant treatment after resection to determine optimal management of such tumors. The databases searched were PubMed, Embase, Ovid (MEDLINE), and Cochrane for articles up to June 19, 2026. A systematic review was conducted. PubMed, Embase, and Ovid (MEDLINE) databases were searched, utilizing keywords such as “Paranasal Sinus Neoplasms” and “Papillomavirus infections”. Reference lists were searched for identification of relevant studies. Case reports, case series, literature reviews, and surgical reports were included. Thirty-one articles were eventually analyzed, with a total of a hundred-and-nineteen HMSC cases reported. The most common treatment prescribed was endoscopic resection. Adjuvant treatment post-surgical resection was administered at similar rates for patients regardless of HMSC staging. The majority of cases were clinically found to have no evidence of disease during their last follow-up, with only 5 cases of mortality due to HMSC reported in the cases that met inclusion criteria. Despite high-grade histological features, HMSC outcomes following definitive treatment are favorable. Endoscopic surgery remains the mainstay of treatment. Without clear guidelines outlining indications for adjuvant treatment, administration was based on the presence of high-risk clinical features. However, the long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates has yet to be discussed. Decisions should be individualized based on margins, invasion, and patient factors. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract To establish outcomes of Human Papillomavirus-Related Multiphenotypic Sinonasal Carcinoma and evaluate indications for adjuvant treatment after resection to determine optimal management of such tumors. The databases searched were PubMed, Embase, Ovid (MEDLINE), and Cochrane for articles up to June 19, 2026. A systematic review was conducted. PubMed, Embase, and Ovid (MEDLINE) databases were searched, utilizing keywords such as “Paranasal Sinus Neoplasms” and “Papillomavirus infections”. Reference lists were searched for identification of relevant studies. Case reports, case series, literature reviews, and surgical reports were included. Thirty-one articles were eventually analyzed, with a total of a hundred-and-nineteen HMSC cases reported. The most common treatment prescribed was endoscopic resection. Adjuvant treatment post-surgical resection was administered at similar rates for patients regardless of HMSC staging. The majority of cases were clinically found to have no evidence of disease during their last follow-up, with only 5 cases of mortality due to HMSC reported in the cases that met inclusion criteria. Despite high-grade histological features, HMSC outcomes following definitive treatment are favorable. Endoscopic surgery remains the mainstay of treatment. Without clear guidelines outlining indications for adjuvant treatment, administration was based on the presence of high-risk clinical features. However, the long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates has yet to be discussed. Decisions should be individualized based on margins, invasion, and patient factors. title_original: Human Papillomavirus-Related Multiphenotypic Sinonasal Carcinoma: A Systematic Review

analysis.scope_and_question: This review focuses on Human Papillomavirus-Related Multiphenotypic Sinonasal Carcinoma (HMSC) and evaluates the outcomes of such tumors, as well as indications for adjuvant treatment after resection to determine optimal management strategies. The central question is about the clinical behavior and treatment approaches for HMSC.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The review searched PubMed, Embase, and Ovid (MEDLINE) databases using keywords like 'Paranasal Sinus Neoplasms' and 'Papillomavirus infections'. It included case reports, case series, literature reviews, and surgical reports. A total of 31 articles were analyzed, with 119 HMSC cases reported.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The majority of HMSC cases showed no evidence of disease during their last follow-up. Endoscopic surgery remains the mainstay of treatment, and adjuvant treatment post-surgical resection was administered at similar rates regardless of HMSC staging. Despite high-grade histological features, outcomes following definitive treatment are favorable.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates has not been discussed. There is no clear guidance on indications for adjuvant treatment, and decisions are based on the presence of high-risk clinical features. The review also notes that the evidence is limited and requires further investigation.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: There is a need for clear guidelines on adjuvant treatment indications for HMSC. Further research is required to understand the long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates. Individualized treatment decisions should be based on margins, invasion, and patient factors.

analysis.summary_en: This systematic review evaluates Human Papillomavirus-Related Multiphenotypic Sinonasal Carcinoma (HMSC), focusing on clinical outcomes and treatment approaches. The review analyzed 31 articles reporting 119 HMSC cases, with endoscopic resection being the primary treatment. Most cases showed no evidence of disease at follow-up, and adjuvant treatment was used similarly across staging groups. Despite high-grade histology, outcomes were favorable. However, the long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence remains unclear. The review highlights the need for individualized treatment decisions and further research to establish guidelines for adjuvant therapy. The findings emphasize the importance of considering patient-specific factors and high-risk clinical features in management strategies.

elements_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点关注 人乳头瘤病毒 相关的多表型鼻窦癌 (HMSC),并评估此类肿瘤的结果,以及切除后辅助 治疗 的适应症,以确定最佳治疗策略。核心问题是关于 HMSC 的临床行为和 治疗 方法。
elements_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述使用“鼻旁窦肿瘤”和“乳头瘤病毒感染”等关键词搜索了 PubMed、Embase 和 Ovid (MEDLINE) 数据库。它包括 病例报告、病例系列、文献综述和手术报告。总共分析了 31 篇文章,报告了 119 例 HMSC 病例。
elements_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 大多数 HMSC 病例在最后一次随访期间没有表现出疾病证据。内窥镜手术仍然是 治疗 的支柱,无论 HMSC 分期如何,辅助 治疗 术后切除的比例相似。尽管具有高级组织学特征,但明确的 治疗 后的结果是有利的。
elements_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 佐剂 治疗 在降低复发率方面的长期作用尚未讨论。对于辅助 治疗 的适应症没有明确的指导,决策基于是否存在高风险临床特征。审查还指出,证据有限,需要进一步调查。
elements_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 需要关于 HMSC 辅助 治疗 适应症的明确指南。需要进一步的研究来了解佐剂 治疗 在降低复发率方面的长期作用。个体化的 治疗 决策应基于切缘、侵袭和患者因素。

analysis_en.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates has not been discussed. There is no clear guidance on indications for adjuvant treatment, and decisions are based on the presence of high-risk clinical features. The review also notes that the evidence is limited and requires further investigation.
analysis_en.research_and_practice_implications: There is a need for clear guidelines on adjuvant treatment indications for HMSC. Further research is required to understand the long-term role of adjuvant treatment in reducing recurrence rates. Individualized treatment decisions should be based on margins, invasion, and patient factors.

analysis_zh.scope_and_question: 本综述重点关注 人乳头瘤病毒 相关的多表型鼻窦癌 (HMSC),并评估此类肿瘤的结果,以及切除后辅助 治疗 的适应症,以确定最佳治疗策略。核心问题是关于 HMSC 的临床行为和 治疗 方法。
analysis_zh.evidence_base_and_review_method: 该综述使用“鼻旁窦肿瘤”和“乳头瘤病毒感染”等关键词搜索了 PubMed、Embase 和 Ovid (MEDLINE) 数据库。它包括 病例报告、病例系列、文献综述和手术报告。总共分析了 31 篇文章,报告了 119 例 HMSC 病例。
analysis_zh.consensus_and_key_conclusions: 大多数 HMSC 病例在最后一次随访期间没有表现出疾病证据。内窥镜手术仍然是 治疗 的支柱,无论 HMSC 分期如何,辅助 治疗 术后切除的比例相似。尽管具有高级组织学特征,但明确的 治疗 后的结果是有利的。
analysis_zh.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: 佐剂 治疗 在降低复发率方面的长期作用尚未讨论。对于辅助 治疗 的适应症没有明确的指导,决策基于是否存在高风险临床特征。审查还指出,证据有限,需要进一步调查。
analysis_zh.research_and_practice_implications: 需要关于 HMSC 辅助 治疗 适应症的明确指南。需要进一步的研究来了解佐剂 治疗 在降低复发率方面的长期作用。个体化的 治疗 决策应基于切缘、侵袭和患者因素。

full_text: BackgroundOropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) has undergone substantial epidemiological and clinical changes, with an increasing proportion of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated tumours and declining tobacco exposure. We investigated temporal changes in patient characteristics, HPV/p16 status, treatment patterns, and survival among patients with OPSCC in Denmark.MethodsPatients with OPSCC were identified from the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database (2000–2023) and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR; 1980–2021). The Copenhagen database provided detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV/p16 status, while the DCR enabled assessment of long-term survival trends. Temporal changes were evaluated across diagnostic periods. Overall survival, relative survival, and restricted mean survival time were estimated.ResultsAmong 3,631 OPSCC patients in the Copenhagen database, median age at diagnosis increased from 59 years in 2000–2005 to 64 years in 2018–2023 (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ patients increased significantly from 43.5% in 2000–2005 to 62.8% in 2018-2023. The proportion of never smokers also increased from 0.5% to 23.5%, while ≥20 pack-years decreased from 73.2% to 52.1% (p<0.001). Treatment patterns changed substantially, with radiotherapy alone decreasing from 87.6% to 27.9% and chemoradiotherapy increasing from 1.6% to 46.3%. Among 9,379 patients in the DCR, five-year relative survival increased from 31.8% in 1980–1984 to 70.1% in 2015-2019. Among HPV+/p16+ patients, five-year overall survival increased from 63.1% in 2000–2005 to 83.7% in 2018–2023.ConclusionIn Denmark, OPSCC has undergone substantial epidemiological and therapeutic changes accompanied by marked improvements in survival, including among HPV+/p16+ patients. MethodStudy designThis study was designed as a retrospective registry-based cohort study with an additional matched population-comparator analysis.ParticipantsWe included patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) in Denmark. Data were obtained from two complementary sources: the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR). The Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database contains patients diagnosed with OPSCC within the Eastern Danish healthcare region and covers the period from 2000 to 2023. The database is updated at three-year intervals and covers approximately half of the Danish population.To extend the study period and identify patients diagnosed prior to establishment of the Copenhagen database, data from the DCR were used for patients diagnosed between 1980 and 2021.Using data from the Danish Civil Registration System, each patient with OPSCC identified in the DCR was matched to 10 population controls based on age, sex, and calendar year of diagnosis. Controls were selected from the Danish general population and were eligible for matching if they were alive and had not been diagnosed with head and neck cancer before the index date. The index date for each control was defined as the corresponding calendar year of diagnosis of OPSCC in the matched patient. Matching was performed without replacement, such that each control could be assigned to only one patient. Patients for whom 10 eligible controls could not be identified were excluded from the matched analysis. Follow-up for patients and matched controls was calculated from the index date until death, emigration, or the end of the study period, whichever occurred first.Data sourcesThe Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database is based on data from the Danish Pathology Registry and the Danish Head and Neck Cancer Group (DAHANCA) database and is supplemented with information extracted from electronic health records (Epic Systems). Patients were identified using their unique Danish personal identification number. Clinical and pathological data were collected in a Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) database at Copenhagen University Hospital – Rigshospitalet, Denmark.Patients with biopsy-confirmed OPSCC diagnosed in Eastern Denmark between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2023, were identified from the DAHANCA database and the Danish Pathology Data Registry. The DAHANCA database prospectively records clinical characteristics of patients with head and neck cancer, while the Danish Pathology Data Registry is a mandatory nationwide registry containing information on tissue samples collected from patients treated in Denmark. Only the first occurring OPSCC were included in this study. Patients were followed from the date of diagnosis (the date of the first biopsy) until death or the end of the follow-up period. Patients who were alive at the last day of follow-up (1/11-24) were censored on that date.For patients diagnosed from 2000 onwards, tumour stage was retrospectively classified according to the UICC 8th edition staging system for p16-positive OPSCC. The available UICC 7th edition N categories were converted as follows: N0 remained N0, N1 remained N1, N2a and N2b were recoded as N1, N2c as N2, and N3 remained N3. For T classification, T4a and T4b were combined into T4. The resulting T and N categories were then used to assign UICC 8th edition stage groups according to the following scheme: stage I for T1–2N0–1, stage II for T1–3N2 and T3N0–1, and stage III for T1–3N3 and all T4 tumours.p16 testingp16 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) using the Ventana Benchmark Ultra autostainer and the p16 monoclonal antibody E6H4 with CC1 pretreatment (Roche, Tucson, AZ, USA) throughout the study period. For tumours diagnosed between 2018 and 2023, the OptiView detection kit was used and tumours were considered p16-positive when >70% of tumour cells showed cytoplasmic and/or nuclear staining. Before 2018, the UltraView detection kit was used and the cutoff for p16 positivity was >75% of tumour cells showing cytoplasmic and nuclear staining.HPV testingFormalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour tissue was used for HPV DNA extraction and asseessment. Different methods were used for HPV DNA evaluation during the study period. For tumours diagnosed between 2021 and 2023 HPV DNA was detected using the VisionArray HPV Chip 1.0 system (ZytoVision, Bremerhaven, Germany), which detects 41 clinically relevant HPV genotypes. The assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions as previously described (2). Samples with discordant HPV and p16 results were retested. For tumours diagnosed between 2018 and 2020, HPV DNA was detected using either a broad-spectrum GP5+/6+ polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay or the VisionArray HPV Chip 1.0. For the GP5+/6+ PCR assay, DNA quality was confirmed using a glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) control, and samples positive for GP5+/6+ and GAPDH were classified as HPV-positive. The method has previously been described (5). Before 2018, HPV DNA was detected using the GP5+/6+ PCR assay. DNA quality was assessed using GAPDH PCR. HPV genotyping was performed by sequencing of GP5+/6+ amplicons using next-generation sequencing, as previously described (9).The DCR includes information on cancer diagnoses, including International Classification of Disease 10 revision (ICD-10) codes, MORPHO3 codes, treatment, and survival outcomes. Patients were identified using relevant ICD-10 diagnosis codes and histological information. The included ICD-10 codes were DC01, DC01.9, DC02.4, DC05.1, DC05.2, DC09, DC09.0–DC09.9, DC10.0, DC10.2, DC10.3, DC10.8, and DC10.9. Histologically, cases were classified as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and thus included based on the following MORPH3 codes: 80303, 80313, 80323, 80333, 80513, 80523, 80703, 80709, 80713, 80719, 80723, 80733, 80743, 80753, 80763, 80823, 80829, 80833, 80843, 80853, 80863, 81213, 81233, 82303, 82309, and 85603. Patients were included if they were registered with an OPSCC in the DCR between 1/1–1980 and 31/12-2020. Only the first occurring OPSCC were included in the study. Patients were followed from the date of diagnosis until death or the end of the follow-up period. Patients who were alive at the last day of follow-up (1/1-24) were censored on that date.The two data sources served complementary purposes: the DCR enabled analyses covering a longer historical period, whereas the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database provided more detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV and p16 status. The specific data source used for each analysis is indicated in the corresponding tables and figures.Study sizeFrom the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database, a total of 3,631 patients were included.A total of 9,057 patients with OPSCC were identified in the DCR. One patient was lost to follow-up and was excluded from the analysis, resulting in a total of 9,056 patients. Eighteen patients emigrated from Denmark during follow-up and were censored at the date of emigration.For the matched analysis, each patient was matched with 10 population controls based on age, sex, and year of diagnosis. Seven patients could not be assigned eligible controls and were therefore excluded from the matched analysis, leaving 9,049 patients for the matched analysis. Of these, eight controls were excluded because they died before the matching date. In total, 90,482 controls were included in the matched analysis.Study outcomesThe primary objective was to characterise temporal changes in the clinical characteristics of patients with OPSCC in parallel with the increasing proportion of HPV-associated disease. The primary outcomes were temporal changes in HPV/p16 status, patient characteristics, tumour stage, and treatment modality. Secondary outcomes included temporal changes in relative survival, overall survival, long-term survival, and survival compared with matched population controls.For temporal analyses, the study periods were divided into approximately equal intervals. For data from the Copenhagen database, the study period was divided into four periods: 2000–2005, 2006–2011, 2012–2017, and 2018–2023. For data from the DCR, the study period was divided into nine periods: 1980–1984, 1985–1989, 1990–1994, 1995–1999, 2000–2004, 2005–2009, 2010–2014, 2015–2019, and 2020–2021 thereby extending the analysis to include the full available study period.Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were used to summarize the study population and tumour characteristics. Categorical variables were presented as numbers and percentages, while continuous variables were summarized using appropriate measures of central tendency and dispersion.Overall survivalOverall survival was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with time calculated from the date of OPSCC diagnosis to the date of death or last available follow-up. Patients who were alive at the end of follow-up were censored at their last known date of follow-up. Kaplan–Meier curves were generated to illustrate overall survival across diagnostic periods, and differences between survival curves were assessed using the log-rank test.Long-term survivalTo assess changes in long-term survival, patients were grouped according to diagnostic period, and Kaplan–Meier estimates of overall survival at 5, 10, and 15 years were calculated. For each survival interval, only patients with sufficient potential follow-up were included. Given follow-up through 2024 (last day of follow-up 1 January 2024), patients diagnosed after 2018, 2013, and 2008 were excluded from the 5-, 10-, and 15-year analyses, respectively. Overall survival at each time point was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with 95% confidence intervals.Relative survivalRelative survival was estimated using data from the DCR to assess survival among patients with OPSCC relative to the expected survival in the general Danish population. Expected survival was derived from Danish population life tables obtained from Statistics Denmark and stratified by age, sex, and calendar year. The relative survival rate was calculated as the ratio of observed to expected survival in Denmark, adjusted for age, sex, and calendar year, using the R package ‘relsurv’. Relative survival curves were estimated using the Ederer II method, with expected survival determined from the population life tables according to age, sex, and calendar year.Survival compared with matched controlsRestricted mean survival time (RMST) was used to quantify differences in survival between patients with OPSCC and matched controls over predefined follow-up periods. This measure represents the expected time alive within a specified follow-up horizon (10). Estimates were obtained at 5, 10, and 15 years after diagnosis for both groups, and the between-group difference in RMST was calculated with corresponding 95% confidence intervals. Thus, the difference in RMST represents the difference in accumulated survival time between patients with OPSCC and their matched controls within each specified time horizon.All statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (version 2025.05.1). Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided P value ≤0.05.ResultsA total of 3,631 patients with OPSCC were included from the Copenhagen database. The median age at diagnosis increased significantly over time, from 59 years (IQR, 52.8–66.0) in 2000–2005 to 64 years (IQR, 57–71) in 2018–2023 (p<0.001). The sex distribution remained stable, with men accounting for approximately 71–74% of patients across all periods (p=0.6) (Table 1). A marked shift in HPV/p16 status was observed over time (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ tumours increased from 43.5% in 2000–2005 to 62.8% in 2018–2023, while the proportion of HPV−/p16− tumours decreased from 40.7% to 24.8%. The proportions of both HPV−/p16+ and HPV+/p16− tumours also decreased over time. The distribution of HPV/p16 status varied by age and diagnosis period (Figure 1). Across all age groups, HPV+/p16+ tumors increased over time, while HPV−/p16− tumors decreased. The increase was most pronounced among patients aged <50 years, with HPV+/p16+ tumors rising from approximately 50% in 2000–2005 to 90% in 2018–2023, compared with an increase from 30% to 60% among full_text_sections.abstract: BackgroundOropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) has undergone substantial epidemiological and clinical changes, with an increasing proportion of human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated tumours and declining tobacco exposure. We investigated temporal changes in patient characteristics, HPV/p16 status, treatment patterns, and survival among patients with OPSCC in Denmark.MethodsPatients with OPSCC were identified from the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database (2000–2023) and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR; 1980–2021). The Copenhagen database provided detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV/p16 status, while the DCR enabled assessment of long-term survival trends. Temporal changes were evaluated across diagnostic periods. Overall survival, relative survival, and restricted mean survival time were estimated.ResultsAmong 3,631 OPSCC patients in the Copenhagen database, median age at diagnosis increased from 59 years in 2000–2005 to 64 years in 2018–2023 (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ patients increased significantly from 43.5% in 2000–2005 to 62.8% in 2018-2023. The proportion of never smokers also increased from 0.5% to 23.5%, while ≥20 pack-years decreased from 73.2% to 52.1% (p<0.001). Treatment patterns changed substantially, with radiotherapy alone decreasing from 87.6% to 27.9% and chemoradiotherapy increasing from 1.6% to 46.3%. Among 9,379 patients in the DCR, five-year relative survival increased from 31.8% in 1980–1984 to 70.1% in 2015-2019. Among HPV+/p16+ patients, five-year overall survival increased from 63.1% in 2000–2005 to 83.7% in 2018–2023.ConclusionIn Denmark, OPSCC has undergone substantial epidemiological and therapeutic changes accompanied by marked improvements in survival, including among HPV+/p16+ patients.
full_text_sections.methods: MethodStudy designThis study was designed as a retrospective registry-based cohort study with an additional matched population-comparator analysis.ParticipantsWe included patients diagnosed with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (OPSCC) in Denmark. Data were obtained from two complementary sources: the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR). The Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database contains patients diagnosed with OPSCC within the Eastern Danish healthcare region and covers the period from 2000 to 2023. The database is updated at three-year intervals and covers approximately half of the Danish population.To extend the study period and identify patients diagnosed prior to establishment of the Copenhagen database, data from the DCR were used for patients diagnosed between 1980 and 2021.Using data from the Danish Civil Registration System, each patient with OPSCC identified in the DCR was matched to 10 population controls based on age, sex, and calendar year of diagnosis. Controls were selected from the Danish general population and were eligible for matching if they were alive and had not been diagnosed with head and neck cancer before the index date. The index date for each control was defined as the corresponding calendar year of diagnosis of OPSCC in the matched patient. Matching was performed without replacement, such that each control could be assigned to only one patient. Patients for whom 10 eligible controls could not be identified were excluded from the matched analysis. Follow-up for patients and matched controls was calculated from the index date until death, emigration, or the end of the study period, whichever occurred first.Data sourcesThe Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database is based on data from the Danish Pathology Registry and the Danish Head and Neck Cancer Group (DAHANCA) database and is supplemented with information extracted from electronic health records (Epic Systems). Patients were identified using their unique Danish personal identification number. Clinical and pathological data were collected in a Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) database at Copenhagen University Hospital – Rigshospitalet, Denmark.Patients with biopsy-confirmed OPSCC diagnosed in Eastern Denmark between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2023, were identified from the DAHANCA database and the Danish Pathology Data Registry. The DAHANCA database prospectively records clinical characteristics of patients with head and neck cancer, while the Danish Pathology Data Registry is a mandatory nationwide registry containing information on tissue samples collected from patients treated in Denmark. Only the first occurring OPSCC were included in this study. Patients were followed from the date of diagnosis (the date of the first biopsy) until death or the end of the follow-up period. Patients who were alive at the last day of follow-up (1/11-24) were censored on that date.For patients diagnosed from 2000 onwards, tumour stage was retrospectively classified according to the UICC 8th edition staging system for p16-positive OPSCC. The available UICC 7th edition N categories were converted as follows: N0 remained N0, N1 remained N1, N2a and N2b were recoded as N1, N2c as N2, and N3 remained N3. For T classification, T4a and T4b were combined into T4. The resulting T and N categories were then used to assign UICC 8th edition stage groups according to the following scheme: stage I for T1–2N0–1, stage II for T1–3N2 and T3N0–1, and stage III for T1–3N3 and all T4 tumours.p16 testingp16 expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) using the Ventana Benchmark Ultra autostainer and the p16 monoclonal antibody E6H4 with CC1 pretreatment (Roche, Tucson, AZ, USA) throughout the study period. For tumours diagnosed between 2018 and 2023, the OptiView detection kit was used and tumours were considered p16-positive when >70% of tumour cells showed cytoplasmic and/or nuclear staining. Before 2018, the UltraView detection kit was used and the cutoff for p16 positivity was >75% of tumour cells showing cytoplasmic and nuclear staining.HPV testingFormalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumour tissue was used for HPV DNA extraction and asseessment. Different methods were used for HPV DNA evaluation during the study period. For tumours diagnosed between 2021 and 2023 HPV DNA was detected using the VisionArray HPV Chip 1.0 system (ZytoVision, Bremerhaven, Germany), which detects 41 clinically relevant HPV genotypes. The assay was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions as previously described (2). Samples with discordant HPV and p16 results were retested. For tumours diagnosed between 2018 and 2020, HPV DNA was detected using either a broad-spectrum GP5+/6+ polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay or the VisionArray HPV Chip 1.0. For the GP5+/6+ PCR assay, DNA quality was confirmed using a glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) control, and samples positive for GP5+/6+ and GAPDH were classified as HPV-positive. The method has previously been described (5). Before 2018, HPV DNA was detected using the GP5+/6+ PCR assay. DNA quality was assessed using GAPDH PCR. HPV genotyping was performed by sequencing of GP5+/6+ amplicons using next-generation sequencing, as previously described (9).The DCR includes information on cancer diagnoses, including International Classification of Disease 10 revision (ICD-10) codes, MORPHO3 codes, treatment, and survival outcomes. Patients were identified using relevant ICD-10 diagnosis codes and histological information. The included ICD-10 codes were DC01, DC01.9, DC02.4, DC05.1, DC05.2, DC09, DC09.0–DC09.9, DC10.0, DC10.2, DC10.3, DC10.8, and DC10.9. Histologically, cases were classified as squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and thus included based on the following MORPH3 codes: 80303, 80313, 80323, 80333, 80513, 80523, 80703, 80709, 80713, 80719, 80723, 80733, 80743, 80753, 80763, 80823, 80829, 80833, 80843, 80853, 80863, 81213, 81233, 82303, 82309, and 85603. Patients were included if they were registered with an OPSCC in the DCR between 1/1–1980 and 31/12-2020. Only the first occurring OPSCC were included in the study. Patients were followed from the date of diagnosis until death or the end of the follow-up period. Patients who were alive at the last day of follow-up (1/1-24) were censored on that date.The two data sources served complementary purposes: the DCR enabled analyses covering a longer historical period, whereas the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database provided more detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV and p16 status. The specific data source used for each analysis is indicated in the corresponding tables and figures.Study sizeFrom the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database, a total of 3,631 patients were included.A total of 9,057 patients with OPSCC were identified in the DCR. One patient was lost to follow-up and was excluded from the analysis, resulting in a total of 9,056 patients. Eighteen patients emigrated from Denmark during follow-up and were censored at the date of emigration.For the matched analysis, each patient was matched with 10 population controls based on age, sex, and year of diagnosis. Seven patients could not be assigned eligible controls and were therefore excluded from the matched analysis, leaving 9,049 patients for the matched analysis. Of these, eight controls were excluded because they died before the matching date. In total, 90,482 controls were included in the matched analysis.Study outcomesThe primary objective was to characterise temporal changes in the clinical characteristics of patients with OPSCC in parallel with the increasing proportion of HPV-associated disease. The primary outcomes were temporal changes in HPV/p16 status, patient characteristics, tumour stage, and treatment modality. full_text_sections.results: ResultsA total of 3,631 patients with OPSCC were included from the Copenhagen database. The median age at diagnosis increased significantly over time, from 59 years (IQR, 52.8–66.0) in 2000–2005 to 64 years (IQR, 57–71) in 2018–2023 (p<0.001). The sex distribution remained stable, with men accounting for approximately 71–74% of patients across all periods (p=0.6) (Table 1). A marked shift in HPV/p16 status was observed over time (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ tumours increased from 43.5% in 2000–2005 to 62.8% in 2018–2023, while the proportion of HPV−/p16− tumours decreased from 40.7% to 24.8%. The proportions of both HPV−/p16+ and HPV+/p16− tumours also decreased over time. The distribution of HPV/p16 status varied by age and diagnosis period (Figure 1). Across all age groups, HPV+/p16+ tumors increased over time, while HPV−/p16− tumors decreased. The increase was most pronounced among patients aged <50 years, with HPV+/p16+ tumors rising from approximately 50% in 2000–2005 to 90% in 2018–2023, compared with an increase from 30% to 60% among full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionIn this study, we observed substantial changes in the epidemiology, treatment, and survival of patients with OPSCC over time.Treatment patterns changed considerably during the study period, with radiotherapy alone becoming less common and combined treatment modality increasing. These changes may reflect advances in the multidisciplinary management of OPSCC, including centralisation of treatment decisions in multidisciplinary tumour boards, refinement of positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-based staging, and the introduction of transoral robotic surgery as a treatment option for selected early-stage tumours (11), although this study did not directly evaluate the drivers of these treatment shifts. Notably, despite the favourable prognosis of HPV+/p16+ OPSCC, treatment de-intensification has not been established as standard practice. Randomised trials evaluating reduced-intensity treatment in this subgroup, including the De-ESCALaTE HPV and Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (RTOG) 1016 trials, failed to demonstrate non-inferiority of cetuximab-based regimens compared with cisplatin-based chemoradiotherapy, and de-escalation therefore remains investigational inside clinical trials (12). This is consistent with continued reliance on combined-modality treatment, rather than de-escalated single-modality regimens, despite the growing proportion of HPV+/p16+ tumours observed in our cohort.Survival improved substantially over the study period. In the DCR cohort, five-year relative survival increased from 31.9% in patients diagnosed in 1980–1984 to 70.1% in those diagnosed in 2015–2019. A similar improvement was observed among HPV+/p16+ patients based on data from the Copenhagen Database, for whom five-year overall survival increased from 63.1% in 2000–2005 to 83.7% in 2018–2023. This improvement is consistent with the established prognostic significance of HPV status first demonstrated by Ang et al. (13), and extends findings from previous Danish nationwide studies reporting improving OPSCC survival over time (5, 8). Importantly, survival also improved within the HPV+/p16+ subgroup, indicating that the increasing proportion of HPV-driven tumours alone does not fully account for the observed population-level improvement in survival. Possible explanations for the remaining improvement include refinements in staging accuracy, changes in patient selection, and improvements in treatment delivery over time. The introduction of HPV-specific staging in the eighth edition of the AJCC/UICC TNM classification during the study period should be considered when interpreting temporal comparisons of stage-stratified outcomes. However, as patients diagnosed from 2000 onwards were retrospectively classified according to UICC 8 using the available UICC 7 T and N categories, differences in stage distribution cannot be attributed solely to the change in staging system. The observed temporal changes may reflect underlying differences in tumour biology and disease presentation, including the increasing proportion of HPV/p16-positive OPSCC. Concurrently, declining tobacco exposure in the general population is likely to have contributed independently to the changing tumour biology (2, 14, 15).The present study builds on previous Danish studies of OPSCC, including the Copenhagen cohort reported by Michaelsen et al. (2) and the nationwide Danish Cancer Registry study by Jakobsen et al (8). While there is substantial cohort overlap, the present study extends these findings by providing a broader longitudinal assessment of clinical characteristics, tumour stage, and treatment patterns, with particular emphasis on long-term survival. The increasing proportion of long-term survivors further demonstrates the substantial improvement in prognosis. However, the comparison with matched population controls showed that patients with OPSCC continued to experience a substantial survival deficit, which increased with longer follow-up. This finding highlighting that improved cancer survival does not necessarily translate into survival comparable to that of the general population. These findings emphasise the growing population of long-term OPSCC survivors and the increasing importance of survivorship and management of late treatment-related effects, including dysphagia, xerostomia, and other functional sequelae of chemoradiotherapy, which can persist for years after treatment completion and substantially affect quality of life (16). This underscores the need for structured, long-term survivorship programmes as an increasing share of the OPSCC population moves from active treatment into extended follow-up.A key strength of this study is the use of two complementary data sources. The evaluation of survival trends over more than four decades was enabled by the DCR, while the Copenhagen database provided detailed clinical and pathological information, including HPV/p16 status. Limitations include limited availability of HPV/p16 data in the DCR, and shorter follow-up in the most recent cohorts. Additionally, changes in staging classification during the study period may limit direct comparability of stage-specific outcomes across diagnostic periods. Further, HPV DNA and p16 status were assessed using different methods and protocols over the study period, including different HPV DNA assays and p16 detection kits and positivity thresholds, which may have introduced some degree of methodological heterogeneity in the classification of HPV/p16 status. Lastly, the completeness of smoking data varied over the study period, and differences in the ascertainment or recording of smoking status over time may have contributed to the observed temporal increase in the proportion of never-smokers. Therefore, this finding should be interpreted with consideration of potential temporal ascertainment bias.In conclusion, OPSCC in Denmark has undergone substantial epidemiological and therapeutic changes, accompanied by marked improvements in both short- and long-term survival. These improvements were also evident among HPV+/p16+ patients, underscoring continued progress in the management of OPSCC. Importantly, the present study demonstrates that these improvements extend to long-term survival and provides insight into survival relative to the Danish general population.

Over the recent decades, HPV-associated OPSCC has emerged as a distinct disease entity, characterised by different patient demographics, tumour biology, risk-factor profiles, and clinical outcomes compared with HPV-negative disease (1).The increasing contribution of HPV to OPSCC has been particularly evident in high-income countries, where the incidence of HPV-positive disease has increased alongside a decline in tobacco-related head and neck cancers (2–4). HPV-positive OPSCC is associated with a more favourable response to treatment and substantially better survival than HPV-negative disease, leading to its recognition as a distinct entity in both the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) and the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) staging systems (1, 5–7). title_original: Changing epidemiology and survival of HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer in Denmark: four decades of population-based data

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to investigate temporal changes in patient characteristics, HPV/p16 status, treatment patterns, and survival among patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer (OPSCC) in Denmark.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Patients with biopsy-confirmed OPSCC diagnosed in Eastern Denmark between January 1, 2000, and December 31, 2023, were identified from the DAHANCA database and the Danish National Patient Cancer Registry (DCR). The two data sources served complementary purposes: the DCR enabled analyses covering a longer historical period, whereas the Copenhagen Oropharyngeal Cancer Database provided more detailed clinical and pathological data, including HPV and p16 status.
analysis.methods: Clinical and pathological data were collected in a Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) database. For tumours diagnosed between 2018 and 2020, HPV DNA was detected using either a broad-spectrum GP5+/6+ polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay or the VisionArray HPV Chip 1.0. DNA quality was confirmed using a glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) control, and samples positive for GP5+/6+ and GAPDH were classified as HPV-positive.
analysis.main_results: Among 3,631 OPSCC patients in the Copenhagen database, median age at diagnosis increased from 59 years in 2000–2005 to 64 years in 2018–2023 (p<0.001). The proportion of HPV+/p16+ patients increased significantly from 43.5% in 2000–2005 to 62.8% in 2018–2023. The proportion of never smokers increased from 0.5% to 23.1%, while the proportion of patients with ≥20 pack-years decreased from 62.4% to 51.7%. Five-year relative survival increased from 31.8% in 1980–1984 to 70.1% in 2015-2019 among 9,379 patients in the DCR. Among HPV+/p16+ patients, five-year overall survival increased from 63.1% in 2000–2005 to 83.7% in 2018–2023.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that OPSCC has undergone substantial epidemiological and therapeutic changes accompanied by marked improvements in survival, including among HPV+/p16+ patients. This finding highlights a significant shift in the disease's characteristics and treatment outcomes over time.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform surveillance and diagnostic strategies for HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer, as well as guide treatment approaches and risk assessment for patients with varying HPV/p16 statuses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is moderate, as it relies on registry data and does not include direct causal relationships or detailed laboratory procedures. The use of different detection kits for p16 and HPV status over time may introduce variability in results.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the changing epidemiology and survival of HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer (OPSCC) in Denmark over four decades. It reports a significant increase in the proportion of HPV+/p16+ patients, a rise in median age at diagnosis, and a marked improvement in survival rates, particularly among HPV+/p16+ individuals. The study highlights shifts in smoking and alcohol patterns, as well as treatment modalities, over time. While the findings suggest substantial changes in disease characteristics and outcomes, the evidence is moderate due to reliance on registry data and potential variability in HPV/p16 detection methods. The results have implications for surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for HPV-associated OPSCC, emphasizing the need for updated approaches in clinical and public health settings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在调查丹麦 HPV 相关口咽癌 (OPSCC) 患者特征、HPV/p16 状态、治疗 模式和生存率的时间变化。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 从 DAHANCA 数据库和丹麦国家患者癌症登记处 (DCR) 中确定了 2000 年 1 月 1 日至 2023 年 12 月 31 日期间在丹麦东部诊断出的经活检确诊为 OPSCC 的患者。这两个数据源具有互补的目的:DCR 能够进行覆盖更长历史时期的分析,而哥本哈根口咽癌数据库提供了更详细的临床和病理数据,包括 HPV 和 p16 状态。
elements_zh.methods: 临床和病理数据收集在研究电子数据捕获(REDCap)数据库中。对于 2018 年至 2020 年间诊断的肿瘤,使用广谱 GP5+/6+ 聚合酶链反应 (PCR) 检测或 VisionArray HPV 芯片 1.0 检测 HPV DNA。使用 3-磷酸甘油醛脱氢酶 (GAPDH) 对照确认 DNA 质量,GP5+/6+ 和 GAPDH 阳性的样本被归类为 HPV 阳性。
elements_zh.main_results: 在哥本哈根数据库中的 3,631 名 OPSCC 患者中,诊断 的中位年龄从 2000-2005 年的 59 岁增加到 2018-2023 年的 64 岁(p<0.001)。HPV+/p16+患者的比例从2000-2005年的43.5%显着增加到2018-2023年的62.8%。从不吸烟者的比例从0.5%增加到23.1%,而≥20包年的患者比例从62.4%下降到51.7%。DCR 的 9,379 名患者的五年相对生存率从 1980-1984 年的 31.8% 增加到 2015-2019 年的 70.1%。在HPV+/p16+患者中,五年总生存率从2000-2005年的63.1%增加到2018-2023年的83.7%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,OPSCC 经历了重大的流行病学和治疗变化,同时生存率显着提高,包括 HPV+/p16+ 患者。这一发现凸显了随着时间的推移,该疾病的特征和 治疗 结果发生了显着变化。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果可为 监测 和 HPV 相关口咽癌的诊断策略提供信息,并指导 治疗 对不同 HPV/p16 状态患者的方法和风险评估。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据是中等的,因为它依赖于注册数据,不包括直接的因果关系或详细的实验室程序。随着时间的推移,使用不同的 p16 和 HPV 状态检测试剂盒可能会导致结果出现差异。

full_text: Abstract Evidence comparing cervical cancer screening strategies that combine artificial intelligence-assisted liquid-based cytology (AI-LBC) and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing in large-scale populations is limited. This study includes 284,002 women who underwent AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping in community-based screening in Wuhan, China. We evaluate the performance of nine hypothesized screening strategies in detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) and their colposcopy referral rates. After correcting for verification bias, HR-HPV testing alone (Strategy 4) demonstrates higher sensitivity (94.93% vs. 83.88%) and a higher Youden’s index (0.864 vs. 0.789) than AI-LBC alone (Strategy 1), but requires a higher referral rate (9.05% vs. 5.49%). Among the triage-based strategies, Strategy 3 (AI-LBC with reflex HR-HPV) achieves a sensitivity of 82.90%, a referral rate of 2.67%, and a Youden’s index of 0.807. HR-HPV genotyping with reflex AI-LBC (Strategy 7) demonstrates a sensitivity of 92.68%, a Youden’s index of 0.899, and a referral rate of 3.34%. Co-testing of AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping (Strategy 9) achieves the highest Youden’s index (0.932), with a sensitivity of 96.37% and a referral rate of 3.70%. These findings suggest that AI-LBC performs well as a standalone screening method, triage tool, or a component a co-testing strategy in cervical cancer screening. When HR-HPV genotyping is available, Strategy 7 or Strategy 9 may be considered, depending on the trade-off between detection performance and referral burden. The authors also acknowledge Wuhan Landing Intelligence Medical Co., Ltd. for its technical support for the AI-LBC system used in this study. title_original: Performance of artificial intelligence-assisted cytology and high-risk human papillomavirus testing for cervical cancer screening

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the performance of cervical cancer screening strategies combining artificial intelligence-assisted liquid-based cytology (AI-LBC) and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing, as evidence comparing these strategies in large-scale populations is limited.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved 284,002 women who underwent AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping in community-based cervical cancer screening in Wuhan, China, between 2019 and 2023.
analysis.methods: The researchers evaluated nine hypothesized screening strategies for detecting cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or worse (CIN2+) and their colposcopy referral rates, using HR-HPV genotyping and AI-LBC as the primary assays, with adjustments for verification bias.
analysis.main_results: HR-HPV testing alone (Strategy 4) showed higher sensitivity (94.93%) and Youden’s index (0.864) than AI-LBC alone (Strategy 1), but required a higher referral rate (9.05%). Co-testing of AI-LBC and HR-HPV genotyping (Strategy 9) achieved the highest Youden’s index (0.932), with a sensitivity of 96.37% and a referral rate of 3.70%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that AI-LBC performs well as a standalone screening method, triage tool, or component of a co-testing strategy, highlighting its potential utility in cervical cancer screening.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results may inform the selection of screening strategies in settings where HR-HPV genotyping is available, balancing detection performance with referral burden for effective cervical cancer prevention.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's design may be limited by potential verification bias, and the results are specific to the Chinese population, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluates nine cervical cancer screening strategies combining artificial intelligence-assisted liquid-based cytology (AI-LBC) and high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) testing in 284,002 women in Wuhan, China. The main results show that HR-HPV testing alone has higher sensitivity and Youden’s index than AI-LBC alone, but requires a higher referral rate. Co-testing of AI-LBC and HR-HPV achieves the highest Youden’s index, with high sensitivity and moderate referral rate. The authors interpret these findings as indicating AI-LBC's effectiveness as a standalone method or triage tool. The study's implications suggest that HR-HPV genotyping with reflex AI-LBC or co-testing may be preferable in settings where HR-HPV is available, depending on the balance between detection performance and referral burden. However, the study's design may be limited by verification bias, and its results may not be generalizable beyond the Chinese population. The evidence is moderate in strength due to these limitations.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估结合人工智能辅助液基细胞学 (AI-LBC) 和高风险 人乳头瘤病毒 (HR-HPV) 检测的 宫颈癌 筛查策略的性能,因为在大规模人群中比较这些策略的证据有限。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及 2019 年至 2023 年间在中国武汉基于社区的 宫颈癌 筛查中接受 AI-LBC 和 HR-HPV 基因分型的 284,002 名女性。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员使用 HR-HPV 基因分型和 AI-LBC 作为主要检测方法,评估了九种假设的检测 2 级或更严重宫颈上皮内瘤变 (CIN2+) 的筛查策略及其阴道镜转诊率,并根据验证偏差进行了调整。
elements_zh.main_results: 单独的 HR-HPV 检测(策略 4)比单独的 AI-LBC(策略 1)显示出更高的敏感性(94.93%)和 Youden 指数(0.864),但需要更高的转诊率(9.05%)。AI-LBC 和 HR-HPV 基因分型联合检测(策略 9)取得了最高的 Youden 指数(0.932),敏感性为 96.37%,转诊率为 3.70%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,AI-LBC 作为独立的筛查方法、分类工具或联合测试策略的组成部分表现良好,突出了其在 宫颈癌 筛查中的潜在效用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果可以为可进行 HR-HPV 基因分型的环境中筛查策略的选择提供参考,平衡检测性能与转诊负担,以实现有效的 宫颈癌 预防。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的设计可能受到潜在验证偏差的限制,并且结果仅针对中国人群,这可能会影响普遍性。由于这些限制,证据的强度中等。
