Prior to electrode patterning, the substrate surface was cleaned by sequential sonication in solvents of increasing polarity. Interdigitated source (S) and drain (D) electrodes were then defined by photolithography, followed by electron-beam evaporation of a Ti/Au bilayer (5 nm/50 nm). The resulting geometry featured a channel length (L) of 5 μm and an effective channel width (W) of 1280 μm, corresponding to the total perimeter of the interdigitated fingers.After electrode fabrication, the substrates were cleaned by sonication in 2-propanol prior to deposition of the organic semiconductor. The transistor channel was formed by spin-coating a poly­(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) solution (4 mg mL–1 in 1,2-dichlorobenzene, filtered through a 0.2 μm membrane) at 2000 rpm for 20 s, followed by thermal annealing at 90 °C for 15 min. The resulting active area was 6.4 × 10–3 cm2.A polystyrene well was glued using polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) over the interdigitated region and filled with 1 mL of HPLC-grade water, serving as the electrolyte gate medium. The gate electrode consisted of a polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) substrate (area ∼0.6 cm2) coated with an Au layer (50 nm) by thermal evaporation.4.7Fabrication of Disposable Gate ElectrodesDisposable gate electrodes were fabricated on PEN substrates by thermal evaporation of gold using a Korvus Thin Film Deposition System (benchtop HEX). The system operates at a base pressure of 5 × 10–6 mbar and accommodates substrates up to 100 mm in diameter. Deposition parameters, including rate and time, were optimized to achieve uniform gold films. Film thickness was monitored in situ using a quartz crystal microbalance (QCM).The electrode geometry consisted of two gold pads (area ∼0.25 cm2) connected by a narrow (0.5 mm) gold track, designed to ensure electrical continuity while defining the active sensing area and the electrical contact region.The electrodes were biofunctionalized with antibody layers (anti-HPV-L1) by drop-casting solutions containing the biorecognition elements. The resulting functionalized electrodes were used as removable gate elements in the SiMoLS device.4.8Device AssemblyThe SiMoLS-based device was electrically interfaced with a PalmSens4 biopotentiostat by connecting the device electrodes to the corresponding PalmSens4 terminals. full_text_sections.conclusion: 3ConclusionsWe report the SiMoLS bioelectronic platform for the ultrasensitive, label-free detection of HPV through the L1 capsid protein. The device (i) achieves detection at 10 zM, with signals beyond the LOD and the LOI (6.4%, corresponding to 3 zM as extrapolated from the Hill-model based fitting curve of Figure d, and 7.8%, corresponding to 4 zMvide supra -, respectively) in a very low sample volumes, and (ii) enables reliable analysis in both model and clinically relevant matrices. The platform provides a complementary approach to nucleic acid–based assays, allowing the detection of active infection without amplification steps. The integration of a biofunctionalized gate within the SiMoLS architecture ensures efficient signal transduction and accurate discrimination between positive and negative samples. Combined with its rapid response, minimal sample preparation, and scalable fabrication, SiMoLS represents a promising strategy for point-of-care HPV screening and early detection applications.
full_text_sections.other: 1IntroductionOncogenic high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) persistence, such as that of HPV-16 and HPV-18, is responsible for the majority of premalignant and malignant epithelial lesions of the cervix and relevant in other types of neoplastic lesions, such as in the anogenital and head-neck areas. Globally, 660k new cases of cervical cancer and 350k deaths were reported in 2022, with nearly 94% of the deaths for cervix cancer occurring in low- and middle-income countries. The World Health Organization (WHO) has set the elimination of cervical cancer by 2030 as a global public health goal, by achieving the following targets known as the “90–70–90” targets. This translates in every country having 90% of girls fully vaccinated against HPV by age 15, 70% of women screened and rescreened by age 35 and 45 respectively, and 90% of women receiving appropriate treatment in regard to pretreatment of cancer and management of invasive cancer.Early detection along with effective management is key to making cervical cancer both preventable and curable. However, global inequities are also reflected in the prevention policies that high-, low- and middle-income countries apply. Differences in prevention policies are also observed in Europe. In Italy, the age-standardized incidence rate of CC is 6.9 per 100,000 women, with 2,400 new cases in 2020. Vaccination against HPV, screening and treatment of precancerous lesions are a cost-effective way to prevent cervical cancer. Indeed, when screening detects an HPV infection or precancerous lesions, these can easily be treated and cancer (with costly surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy) can be avoided. The high burden costs for National Health Services in the vaccination may not be sustainable, thus making the development of point-of-care testing (POCT) platforms capable of rapid, large-scale screening and early detection of infected individuals crucial for enabling timely therapeutic intervention and improving clinical outcomes.Current HPV screening strategies are primarily based on the sampling of cervical cells. The analysis of cervical brush samples targets viral DNA or mRNA from high-risk HPV strains through amplification techniques such as Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). These approaches are highly sensitive, though requiring costly and time-consuming procedures (3 h), with specialized personnel needed and can be mostly affected by the amplification of interferents contained in the biological sample.Similar challenges arise in the detection of HPV in the head-neck HPV-related cancers. Usually diagnosed at an advanced stage, the viral load in saliva is often low, making the detection in saliva and its reliable identification still a challenge. In this context, protein-based immunometric detection offers a complementary approach to those techniques that rely on the detection and amplification of genomic sequences by enabling direct identification of viral components associated with active infection. The HPV-16 L1 capsid protein, which is abundantly expressed during productive infection in differentiated epithelial layers, represents a relevant structural biomarker. Its expression is typically low in basal cells and may decrease in advanced lesions, reflecting disruption of the viral life cycle. Therefore, targeting HPV-16 L1 is suited for identifying early or active stages of infection, especially in biological samples where viral concentration is limited. − The use of protein biomarkers could also improve the detection in subjects at greatest risk for developing cervical cancer as reported by Brown et al., and thus addresses the need for technologies capable of detecting HPV infections at the single-molecule level in the head-neck area and in those cases where very low analyte concentrations are found in clinically relevant samples. Recent reviews have further highlighted the growing interest in protein biomarkers as complementary tools for the diagnosis, prognosis, and risk stratification. Lately, we have introduced the Singe-Molecule with a Large Surface (SiMoLS) platform for the detection at ultralow concentrations. This stems from our seminal work centered on bioelectronic detection also applied to viral , and bacterial sensing. Such innovative bioelectronic platforms based on transistor technology have recently emerged as a promising approach for ultrasensitive biomarker detection. The SiMoLS hand-held device has demonstrated the capability (i) to be an easy-to-use antigenic test for the early assay of viruses, and (ii) to detect clinically relevant analytes at the physical limit in sample volumes of 0.1 mL, achieving false positive and false negative rates below 1%. These studies demonstrate the versatility of the SiMoLS platform for detecting low-abundance targets in biological matrices. Thus, extending our approach to HPV represents a logical step, particularly for targeting structural proteins such as HPV-16 L1.The present study aims to integrate selective capture antibodies for HPV assays into a SiMoLS-based technology, enabling single-molecule detection of HPV markers and viral particles in both reference fluids and clinical samples added with HPV-16 L1. The platform is designed to achieve highly reliable, noninvasive detection of single or few viral entities in as little as 0.1 mL of brushing specimens, targeting false-positive and false-negative rates below 1%. full_text: AbstractPersistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is the primary cause of cervical cancer (CC). However, most HPV infections are transient and are cleared by effective host immune responses. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms that allow viral persistence and immune escape is critical to explaining why only a subset of women develops cervical lesions and invasive cancer. Although cervical cancer is largely preventable through vaccination and screening, it remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality among women worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. This significant disparity underscores the ongoing inequities in access to HPV vaccination, screening, and timely treatment, which hinder the World Health Organization aim to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health concern by 2030. This narrative review examines how viral, host, and microenvironmental factors interact to promote HR-HPV persistence and cervical cancer development, with particular attention to evidence from Mexican women. HR-HPV can evade immune surveillance by interfering with innate immune recognition, interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and cytotoxic lymphocyte activity. These alterations are compounded by cervicovaginal dysbiosis, immunosuppressive cytokines, regulatory-cell expansion, host genetic variation, and altered microRNA expression. Together, these interconnected processes impair viral clearance and create conditions that favor the progression of cervical lesions to invasive cancer. A comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms may facilitate the identification of biomarkers of HPV persistence and disease progression, while supporting the development of more effective immunotherapeutic strategies and precision prevention approaches, particularly for populations disproportionately affected by cervical cancer.Keywords: cervical cancer, HPV persistence, human papillomavirus, human papillomavirus immune response, tumor microenvironment 1.Literature search strategyA structured literature search was conducted in PubMed between August 2025 and August 2026 to identify scientific literature addressing the molecular and immunological mechanisms underlying high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) persistence and cervical carcinogenesis. Search terms included combinations of “human papillomavirus,” “HPV,” or “high-risk HPV” with terms related to viral persistence and carcinogenesis, viral immune evasion and HPV proteins, innate and adaptive immunity, cytokines and immune checkpoints, cervicovaginal microbiota, host genetic, microRNA-related factors, public health, vaccination, and therapeutics.Only English-language scientific publications were considered, including original research articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and relevant narrative reviews. Seminal studies were retained when necessary to describe established molecular and immunological mechanisms, while recent evidence was incorporated to reflect current advances. The scientific literature search was complemented by official reports and publicly available resources from international health and cancer surveillance organizations to obtain epidemiological data and information on HPV vaccination and cervical cancer prevention and elimination strategies. Studies and institutional sources were selected according to their relevance to the scope of the review. As this was a narrative review, no formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative evidence synthesis was performed. 2.IntroductionCervical cancer (CC) remains a significant global health issue, with approximately 600,000 new cases and 280,000 deaths estimated worldwide in 2024 (1). More than 200 types of human papillomavirus (HPV) have been identified and are classified according to their oncogenic potential. Low-risk HPV types are primarily associated with benign lesions, such as anogenital warts, whereas high-risk HPV (HR-HPV) types are associated with cervical intraepithelial lesions and cervical cancer (2). Among the carcinogenic HPV types, HPV16 and HPV18 are particularly relevant, as they account for the majority of HPV-positive invasive cervical cancers worldwide (3–5). Although HPV infection is common among sexually active individuals, most newly acquired infections are transient and resolve spontaneously. In contrast, persistent HR-HPV infection increases the risk of developing cervical intraepithelial lesions and, eventually, cervical cancer (6–8).The prevalence of HPV infection differs by age and geographic region. It is generally higher among younger women, with a first peak before 25 years of age, although age-specific patterns vary across populations (9). Despite the widespread implementation of HPV vaccination and cervical cancer screening programs, the disease continues to pose a major public health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where access to prevention and treatment remains limited (10). Women living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are also at substantially greater risk of developing cervical cancer (11). These differences in age, geographic setting, immune status, and access to preventive healthcare are important considerations for understanding why some HPV infections persist and progress toward cervical cancer.The outcome of HPV infection is largely determined by the dynamic interplay between viral immune evasion strategies and the host immune response. HR-HPV has evolved sophisticated mechanisms to evade both innate and adaptive immunity, primarily through the activities of the early proteins E5, E6, and E7, which interfere with pathogen recognition receptor signaling, type I interferon responses, antigen processing and presentation, and immune cell activation (12). Persistent HR-HPV infection progressively remodels the local immune microenvironment, promoting immune suppression and creating conditions that favor viral persistence, lesion progression, and malignant transformation (12, 13). Among HR-HPV-positive women, high parity, long-term oral contraceptive use, smoking, and coinfection with other sexually transmitted agents have been identified as potential cofactors associated with progression to High-Grade Squamous Intraepithelial Lesion (HSIL) and invasive cervical cancer (14). full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractPersistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is the primary cause of cervical cancer (CC). However, most HPV infections are transient and are cleared by effective host immune responses. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms that allow viral persistence and immune escape is critical to explaining why only a subset of women develops cervical lesions and invasive cancer. Although cervical cancer is largely preventable through vaccination and screening, it remains a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality among women worldwide, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. This significant disparity underscores the ongoing inequities in access to HPV vaccination, screening, and timely treatment, which hinder the World Health Organization aim to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health concern by 2030. This narrative review examines how viral, host, and microenvironmental factors interact to promote HR-HPV persistence and cervical cancer development, with particular attention to evidence from Mexican women. HR-HPV can evade immune surveillance by interfering with innate immune recognition, interferon signaling, antigen presentation, and cytotoxic lymphocyte activity. These alterations are compounded by cervicovaginal dysbiosis, immunosuppressive cytokines, regulatory-cell expansion, host genetic variation, and altered microRNA expression. Together, these interconnected processes impair viral clearance and create conditions that favor the progression of cervical lesions to invasive cancer. A comprehensive understanding of these mechanisms may facilitate the identification of biomarkers of HPV persistence and disease progression, while supporting the development of more effective immunotherapeutic strategies and precision prevention approaches, particularly for populations disproportionately affected by cervical cancer.Keywords: cervical cancer, HPV persistence, human papillomavirus, human papillomavirus immune response, tumor microenvironment

Seminal studies were retained when necessary to describe established molecular and immunological mechanisms, while recent evidence was incorporated to reflect current advances. The scientific literature search was complemented by official reports and publicly available resources from international health and cancer surveillance organizations to obtain epidemiological data and information on HPV vaccination and cervical cancer prevention and elimination strategies.
